lessons.notes_html:
The word science comes from the Latin word Scientia, which means knowledge or learning. Science is the knowledge in which we study the things around us, or the principles of nature, and try to prove these observations by experiments to get logical results.

Definition of Biology

The word Biology is derived from two Greek words: bios means life and logos means study. So the scientific study of life or living organisms is called biology, or biological science, or life science. Biology is a significant part of everyday life: progress in biology gives us better quality of food, improved health facilities and a hygienic environment.

The Quran Instructs Us to Study Life

Many Quranic injunctions stress the study of biology. These verses describe the study of organisms and their different aspects of life:

  • Origin of Life — Modern biologists believe that life originated first in oceans and then migrated to land. Allah says in the Holy Quran that every living thing was made from water (Surah Al-Ambiya-21: Verse-30), and that man was made from a clattering clay like the earthen ware (Surah Al-Rehman-55: Verse-14).
  • Pairs of Plants and Animals — Plants and animals have male and female partners, and new generations are formed by sexual reproduction. "And of everything created we opposite kinds (pairs)" (Surah Al-Zariyat-51: Verse-49).
  • Communal Life — Animals of the same species live together in the form of a population, and different populations live in the form of a community (Surah Al-Anaam-6: Verse-38).
  • Human Embryology — Many verses stress the study of the different stages of the embryo: "He creates you in your mother's womb in one manner of creation after the other in three folds shadow" (Surah Al-Zamar-39: Verse-6).
  • Locomotion in Animals — Some verses explain locomotion: some animals walk upon their bellies, some upon two feet and some upon four (Surah Al-Nur-24: Verse-45).
  • Flight of Birds — "Do they not see the birds above them spreading their wings and closing them? No one holds them but the All-Merciful" (Surah Al-Mulk-67: Verse-19).

Key Points

  • Science (Scientia) means knowledge gained by observations proved through experiments.
  • Biology = bios (life) + logos (study): the scientific study of living organisms.
  • The Quran repeatedly instructs the study of life: origin of life, pairs, communal life, embryology, locomotion and flight of birds.

lessons.notes_html:
To study the different aspects of all living organisms, the science of Biology is divided into many fields and branches.

Three Major Fields of Biology

  • Microbiology — The scientific study of microorganisms (e.g. bacteria).
  • Botany — The scientific study of plants.
  • Zoology — The scientific study of animals.

Branches of Biology

  • Cytology (Cell Biology) — Study of all aspects of the structure and function of cells.
  • Embryology — Study of the development of an embryo to a complete individual.
  • Genetics — Study of genes, genetic variation and heredity in living organisms.
  • Molecular Biology — Study of the structure, composition and interaction of molecules found in organisms.
  • Pathology — Study of the causes and treatment of diseases in organisms.
  • Ecology — Study of the relationship between an organism and its environment.
  • Marine Biology — Study of organisms found in oceans.
  • Immunology — Study of the immune system, or immunity of a body against pathogens.
  • Morphology — Scientific study of the form and external structure of living organisms.
  • Anatomy — Study of the internal structures of living organisms.
  • Histology — Microscopic study of tissues of animals and plants.
  • Physiology — Study of the functions of the different parts of living organisms.
  • Taxonomy — Study of identification, naming and classification of living organisms into groups and subgroups.
  • Palaeontology — Study of fossils. It has two branches: Palaeobotany (plant fossils) and Palaeozoology (animal fossils).
  • Pharmacology — Study of drugs and their effects on the cell, tissue, organ or organism.
  • Biotechnology — Use of living organisms, cells or biological systems to form useful products to improve human life, agriculture or environment.

Key Points

  • The three major fields of biology are Microbiology, Botany and Zoology.
  • Each branch studies one aspect of life, from cells (cytology) and tissues (histology) to fossils (palaeontology) and drugs (pharmacology).

lessons.notes_html:
In biology we study living organisms, yet it is also related with other branches of science. Many new branches of science have been developed by the combination of biology with other sciences.

Relationship of Biology with Other Sciences

  • Biophysics — Methods and principles from physics are used to study the mechanisms of biological systems, e.g. the principle of lever explains the movement of arms and legs joints.
  • Biochemistry — The chemical processes and substances within living organisms: compositions and chemical reactions of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.
  • Computational Biology — Computational techniques are used to understand and analyze biological systems.
  • Biogeography — Study of the geographical distribution of living organisms. A camel lives successfully in a warm desert and a polar bear in cold areas.
  • Biostatistics (Biometry) — Statistical methods are used to analyze the different aspects in biology.
  • Bioeconomics — Study of living resources using principles of economics, e.g. the cost value and profit value of the poultry business can be calculated.

Careers in Biology

  • Medicine and Surgery — Medicine deals with the diagnosis and treatment of human diseases; surgery with the repairing, replacement and removal of different body parts. After MBBS, doctors specialize as physicians, heart specialists, eye specialists and surgeons. BDS and DVM are also medical professions.
  • Agriculture — Cultivation of plants for food, biofuel, fibre and other products. Agriculturists work for the improvement of crops like wheat, rice and corn.
  • Horticulture — The science of growing gardens, fruits, vegetables, flowers and ornamental plants.
  • Forestry — Study of the production of artificial forest in an area along with the protection of natural forest; important for timber, biodiversity management and habitat for wildlife.
  • Animal Husbandry — Professional study of the care, improvement and breeding of livestock (domestic animals) e.g. cow, goat, sheep.
  • Farming — Developing different types of farms e.g. poultry, vegetable, fruit, animal breeding, fish and dairy farms.
  • Fisheries — Study of the production of animals on commercial scale obtained from sea or rivers, e.g. fish, prawns and lobsters.

Biology: A Part of Natural and Life Science

Natural science deals with the study of all aspects of the natural world in a scientific way; its main branches are Physics, Chemistry, Geology, Astronomy and Biology. Biology is a part of natural science because it helps us understand living things: when we study how plants make their own food by photosynthesis, we are learning a natural process. Life science is a vast field dealing with living organisms and the associated knowledge of factors which influence living organisms; the study of the human immune system, for example, uses cytology, microbiology, genetics and physiology together.

Science is a Collaborative Field

Science is a collaborative field that requires interdisciplinary researchers working together to share knowledge and critique ideas. In biotechnology, an organism or the system of an organism is used to produce useful products for humanity on a large scale, e.g. insulin is commercially prepared from bacteria using modern technology. Research in cancer needs the collaboration of biologists, chemists, physicists and pharmacists together.

Key Points

  • Biophysics, Biochemistry, Computational Biology, Biogeography, Biostatistics and Bioeconomics join biology with other sciences.
  • Biology opens careers in medicine, agriculture, horticulture, forestry, animal husbandry, farming and fisheries.
  • Biology is both a natural science and a life science, and modern science advances by collaboration.

lessons.notes_html:
Scientists work in a systematic way to get the answers to their questions. They want to get a solid answer about a problem without any doubt.

Biological Problem and Biological Method

A problem caused by a living organism or environmental factor that has harmful effects on other living ones is called a biological problem. The systematic procedure adopted by biologists to get a possible answer or solution of a biological problem is called the biological method. It consists of detection of problem, observation, hypothesis, deduction, experiment, theory and finally to develop a scientific law.

Steps Involved in the Biological Method

  • 1. Recognition — When biologists come across a biological problem, they detect it carefully, using all five senses to know the nature of the problem.
  • 2. Observations — The first phase to solve a problem: the biologist uses all sources to get information. Qualitative observations deal only with qualities or properties; Quantitative observations deal with numerical data. Noting the type of disease in plants of an area is qualitative; recording the number of healthy and diseased plants is quantitative.
  • 3. Hypothesis — A possible answer to a biological problem: a simple logical but untested statement which may be the solution. A good hypothesis helps a biologist to make a prediction. It is derived from observations arranged in the form of data, after deep thinking, discussions and reasoning.
  • 4. Prediction / Deduction — After careful and logical thinking, a biologist selects a hypothesis that may be true. Deduction is a possible specific belief about the solution, based on the "if" and "then" format.
  • 5. Experiment / Testing — The hypothesis may be true or wrong, so it is tested by experiments. An incorrect hypothesis is rejected and a new hypothesis is formulated. The hypothesis is accepted only when proved by experiments, carried out many times. In experiments, the control group is not exposed to the factor being tested, while the experimental group is exposed to it, so the results can be compared.
  • Analysis and Reporting the Results — After the experiments, biologists collect the facts or figures in the form of data, analyze the results statistically and decide what actions to take next. After reaching a conclusion, biologists share their views by publishing their work as research papers in scientific journals or in books. Publishing is an integral part of a biological method.
  • 6. Scientific Theory — When a hypothesis is proved by a series of experiments, it is called a scientific theory. It remains valid as long as there is no evidence to disprove it. A theory which gives the final solution and may suggest new hypotheses is called a productive theory.
  • 7. Scientific Law — When a productive theory is established and satisfies other hypotheses, it becomes a scientific law. Scientific laws are always true, in the form of short statements and universally accepted, e.g. Mendel's laws of inheritance.

The steps of the biological method, from recognition of the problem to a scientific law.

Key Points

  • Biological method: recognition, observation, hypothesis, deduction, experiments, theory, law.
  • Observations are qualitative (qualities) or quantitative (numbers and data).
  • A hypothesis proved again and again becomes a theory; an established theory becomes a law.

lessons.notes_html:
Malaria is a common example of a biological problem. It is commonly called "chill and fever disease". According to the old belief, the bad air of swampy places was responsible for this disease — the name malaria is derived from two Italian words: "Mala" means bad and "aria" means air.

Recognition and Observations

In 1878, Laveran (a French Army physician) worked on the cause of malaria. He observed some tiny living creatures in the blood of malarial patients; later other physicians also noticed these tiny creatures in the blood of other malarial patients. They called them plasmodium. The observations of different biologists were:

  • People living near marshes are mostly affected by malaria.
  • Malaria is not caused by drinking marsh water.
  • Plasmodia are found in the blood of all malarial patients.
  • Malaria is treated only by quinine.

Hypothesis and Deduction

On the basis of these observations, a logical hypothesis was formulated: "Malaria is caused by plasmodium." The deduction was stated as: "If malaria is due to plasmodium, then all the malarial patients should have plasmodium in their blood."

Experiments and Conclusion

Biologists tested this deduction by experiments. The blood of a hundred malarial patients (experimental group) and a hundred healthy persons (control group) was observed under the microscope. The blood of all the patients had plasmodia, while plasmodia were not found in the blood of 97 healthy persons — and those few healthy persons who had plasmodia were in the incubation period (the time between the entry of the parasite in the host and the appearance of symptoms), so they became malarial patients in the near future. Ronald Ross (a British Army physician) proved by experiments that female mosquitoes get plasmodia from malarial patients and transmit them to healthy persons. The work of different biologists finally proved that plasmodium is the cause of malaria, and the female Anopheles mosquito transmits plasmodium from patient to healthy person. (The male anopheles does not suck blood; the female sucks human blood to get red blood cell protein, which is needed for the maturation of her eggs.)

Role of Hypothesis, Theory and Law in Research

  • Hypothesis — A possible answer to a problem; the first step of scientific research. It provides a base to predict the possible solution and guides a scientist to collect the facts to prove it.
  • Theory — An experimentally proved hypothesis. The process of theory development involves observations, deductions and experiments. It is a well established and logical explanation of a problem, a generalized principle and the backbone of scientific understanding, e.g. cell theory and theory of evolution.
  • Law — An experimentally proved theory that gives the final solution of a problem without any doubt. Laws are solid explanations, always true and often expressed mathematically, e.g. Mendel's laws of inheritance.

Key Points

  • Laveran (1878) first saw plasmodium in the blood of malarial patients.
  • Experiments on 100 patients and 100 healthy persons proved plasmodium causes malaria.
  • Ronald Ross proved the female Anopheles mosquito transmits malaria.

lessons.notes_html:
All organisms are chemically made up of biological molecules or biomolecules, which include proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids. Protoplasm is the living content of the cell that is surrounded by a plasma membrane; it is a general term for cytoplasm and nucleoplasm.

Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

  • Biochemistry — Deals with the study of chemical compounds and the chemical reactions occurring in living organisms. It is a combination of biology and chemistry, so it is also called biological chemistry. It explains the chemical composition of living organisms and the vital processes occurring in them, e.g. respiration and photosynthesis.
  • Molecular Biology — Explains the structure, composition and interactions of macromolecules (protein, lipid, nucleic acids etc.) present in living organisms.

The Four Common Biomolecules

BiomoleculeWhat it isMain roles
ProteinsThe most abundant biomolecules in living bodies, made up of smaller units called amino acids. Sources: fish, egg, beef.Help in building and repairing of tissues. Enzymes are proteins, which regulate chemical reactions in organisms. Important constituents of cell membrane, ribosomes, mitochondria and chromosomes.
CarbohydratesNature's most abundant biomolecules, composed of C, H and O in the ratio of 1 : 2 : 1; general formula CH2O. Sources: sugar, potato, rice, cotton.The main role is to provide energy (ATP) by the breakdown of glucose. They are the principal source of energy. Present in membranous organelles, and also found in RNA and DNA.
LipidsHeterogeneous biomolecules in nature. Sources: fats, oils, butter.Help the movement of materials in and out of the cells. They are the reserve energy source in the body. Constituents of membranous organelles e.g. mitochondria, Golgi bodies, lysosomes.
Nucleic AcidsVery important biomolecules made up of smaller units called nucleotides. Present in all living organisms as well as viruses. Two types: DNA and RNA.DNA is present in the nucleus of the cell, coiled over the protein to form chromosomes; it is also found in mitochondria and chloroplast. Genes, the units of heredity, are composed of DNA and control the production of specific proteins. RNA is mainly found in the cytoplasm (also in nucleolus, ribosomes, mitochondria and chloroplast) and plays a very important role in protein synthesis.

Key Points

  • Biochemistry studies the chemistry of life; molecular biology studies macromolecules and their interactions.
  • The four biomolecules are proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids.

lessons.notes_html:
In 1838, Berzelius suggested the name protein, derived from the Greek word "Proteios" which means first or prime. Proteins are very important organic compounds of the cell and comprise over 50% of the total dry weight of the cell.

Sources of Proteins

There are two main sources of proteins, i.e. animals and plants. Animal sources include mutton, beef, chicken, fish, egg and milk. Plant sources include beans, peas, spinach, pumpkins, pumpkin seeds and dry fruits (almond, peanuts) etc.

Amino Acids: The Building Blocks

Proteins are made up of amino acids, the structural units or building blocks of proteins. Most protein molecules have 300 to 3000 amino acids. Most proteins are made up of 20 common types of amino acids, e.g. alanine, glycine and valine. All amino acids are built on a common plan: each contains a central carbon atom called the "Alpha Carbon" bonded with a hydrogen atom (H), an amino group (–NH2), a carboxyl group (–COOH) and a variable group (R). Amino acids mainly differ due to the nature of the R-group, which determines the individual chemical properties of the amino acid. In glycine the R-group is a hydrogen atom; in alanine it is CH3.

The Peptide Bond

In a protein molecule, the amino acids are arranged like beads on a string, linked by peptide bonds. A peptide bond forms when the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next amino acid: an OH is released from the COOH of one amino acid while an H+ is released from the NH2 group of the adjacent amino acid, so a water molecule is released, forming a bond between N and C called the peptide bond. For example, glycine and alanine combine to form glycylalanine (a dipeptide).

Functions of Proteins

  • Proteins are involved in the synthesis of every part of the cell, for example nuclear membrane, ribosome, mitochondria, chromosomes and lysosomes.
  • Enzymes are also proteins and are very important for the chemical reactions in the cell.
  • Our muscles, nails and skin are all made of protein.
  • Haemoglobin, a protein found in blood, carries oxygen to all parts of the body; it also transports a part of CO2.
  • Proteins are the important source of human food (meat, beef, fish) and help in the repairing and building of body tissues.

Vitamins are organic substances that are essential for normal growth and nutrition. They are needed in minute quantities in the diet, act especially as coenzymes in the metabolic process, but do not provide energy or serve as building units.

Key Points

  • Proteins (Proteios = first) make over 50% of the dry weight of a cell.
  • Amino acids join by peptide bonds, releasing a water molecule at each bond.
  • Enzymes and haemoglobin are important proteins.

lessons.notes_html:
Lipids are heterogeneous oily bio-molecules. The main sources of lipids are animals and plants. Important animal sources are fatty meat, fatty fish (e.g. salmon), milk, egg and dairy products (yogurt, butter, ghee, cheese). Plant sources are corn, peanuts, dry fruits (walnut, pistachio, almond), coconut etc. Oil is obtained from the seeds of many plants, for example soyabean, sunflower, coconut and cotton.

Composition of Lipids

Lipids are composed of C, H and O, but the proportion of oxygen is less as compared to carbohydrates. There are many types of lipids, but the most abundant lipids in living organisms are fats and oil. A neutral fat is formed by the combination of two compounds, i.e. glycerol and fatty acid.

  • Glycerol — It consists of a chain of three carbon atoms. Each carbon has one hydroxyl group (OH).
  • Fatty Acid — It is a long straight chain of carbon atoms with a carboxylic group (COOH) at one end. There are single covalent bonds between carbon and hydrogen atoms.
  • Triglycerol — A common lipid, formed by the combination of one glycerol and three fatty acids with the release of three H2O molecules.

Functions of Lipids

  • Lipids are the reserve energy source in the body. Lipids provide 9 Kcal/gm energy, while proteins and carbohydrates provide 4 Kcal/gm energy.
  • Butter and ghee are important in the human diet.
  • Lipids help in the transportation of materials in and out of the cells.
  • Prostaglandins, hormone-like compounds that control blood pressure and regulate the contraction and relaxation of smooth muscles, are lipid in nature.
  • Lipids combine with other molecules to form conjugated molecules; for example, phospholipids are important constituents of the cell membrane.
  • Vitamin A and D are also lipid in nature. The deficiency of vitamin A causes night blindness; vitamin "D" is necessary for bone growth.

From the liver of cod fish, an oil called cod liver oil is obtained, which contains vitamin A and D that keep our immune system strong. But too much fat in the diet makes a person obese and also causes cardiovascular disorders like high blood pressure and heart attack.

Key Points

  • A fat = one glycerol + three fatty acids − three water molecules (a triglyceride).
  • Lipids are the reserve energy store and give 9 Kcal per gram.
  • Phospholipids build cell membranes; vitamins A and D are lipids.

lessons.notes_html:
Carbohydrates are complex biomolecules made of C, H and O in the ratio of 1 : 2 : 1. Their general formula is CH2O; for example, glucose is C6H12O6. These are commonly called sugars. Carbohydrates are mostly obtained from plants, for example sugarcane, potato, carrot, cereals (wheat, rice, beans, barley, corn, grams etc.) and fruits (grapes, mango, pineapple). Milk is the only considerable example of an animal source of carbohydrates. Carbohydrates are 50–80% of the plant's dry weight, while there is less than 1% CH2O in the bodies of animals.

Functions of Carbohydrates

  • Carbohydrates are the main source of energy in living organisms. This energy (ATP) is generated during respiration by the breakdown of glucose with oxygen.
  • Carbohydrates are stored in plants in the form of starch and are the important source of human diet, for example potato, rice, corn and sugarcane.
  • Carbohydrates are the constituents of nucleic acids: ribose sugar in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA.
  • Glucose is the major product of photosynthesis, and the life of other organisms directly or indirectly depends upon autotrophic plants.
  • Carbohydrates combine with other compounds to form glycoproteins and glycolipids, the constituents of the plasma membrane, and provide energy for cell division.

Types of Carbohydrates

  • A) Monosaccharides (Simplest Sugar) — True carbohydrates: simple sugars with only one saccharide molecule (3–7 carbon). They are colourless, crystalline solids, sweet in taste and easily soluble in water. Their general formula is CnH2nOn, for example glucose and fructose.
  • B) Disaccharides — Made up of two monosaccharide units. The most common disaccharides found in nature are maltose, lactose and sucrose. They are less sweet in taste and less soluble in water than monosaccharides. Their general formula is C12H22O11, and they give two monosaccharide units on hydrolysis. Maltose is formed by the union of two glucose molecules forming a glycosidic linkage: Glucose + Glucose → Maltose + H2O. Sucrose (Table Sugar) is formed by the union of glucose and fructose forming a glucosidic linkage: Glucose + Fructose → Sucrose + H2O.
  • C) Polysaccharides — Contain a large number of monosaccharide units (more than 10). These are the most common and complex carbohydrates in nature. Their general formula is (C6H10O5)n. They are not very reactive chemically, usually have branched structure, and are non-crystalline, tasteless and insoluble in water but sparingly soluble in hot water, e.g. cellulose and starch.

Key Points

  • Carbohydrates: C, H, O in 1 : 2 : 1 ratio; the main energy source of the cell.
  • Monosaccharides (one unit), disaccharides (two units), polysaccharides (many units).
  • Maltose = glucose + glucose; Sucrose = glucose + fructose.

lessons.notes_html:
DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid) is a polynucleotide chain made up of many nucleotides. Each nucleotide is itself a complex compound composed of three components:

  • 1. Nitrogenous bases — These are of two types: (a) Purine (Adenine, Guanine); (b) Pyrimidine (Cytosine, Thymine).
  • 2. Pentose (5-carbon) Sugar — Deoxyribose sugar.
  • 3. Phosphate group (–PO4)

In a DNA molecule there are four types of nucleotides, named due to the nitrogenous base they contain: Adenine nucleotide, Guanine nucleotide, Cytosine nucleotide and Thymine nucleotide.

The Watson and Crick Model of DNA

James Watson (an American biologist) and Francis Crick (an English chemist) designed a model of DNA in 1953; for this unique work they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1962. Each DNA molecule is made up of two polynucleotide chains or strands which run in opposite direction to each other, twisted into a double helix. The backbone of the ladder (chains) is made of alternately arranged units of phosphate group and pentose sugar. One complete turn of the helix has ten base pairs and is 3.4 nm in length. The diameter of the DNA molecule is about 2 nm (20 Å). The two chains are linked, just like rungs (steps) in a ladder, by the pairs of bases (Purines and Pyrimidines). Each rung consists of a purine matched with a pyrimidine. The matching of the bases is highly specific, i.e. A = T and C ≡ G. In a DNA molecule, the amount of adenine is equal to that of thymine and the amount of guanine is equal to that of cytosine.

The DNA ladder: two strands joined by specific base pairs.

Function of DNA

DNA is the hereditary material. It transfers characters from parents to offsprings, for example skin colour and blood groups. DNA controls the development and functioning of all living organisms. The transfer of hereditary information is carried out by genes: a gene is the short specific portion of DNA, and it is the unit of heredity. Each gene contains instructions to build specific proteins, and the proteins are responsible for traits and functions in the body. The arrangement of bases (A, G, C, T) in a gene is highly specific; any change in the base arrangement will change the gene. This change is called mutation. Due to mutation, faulty information is transferred to the next generation and the structure of the protein changes — for example, in sickle cell anemia the shape and function of RBCs change due to the replacement of only one amino acid (glutamic acid) out of 574 by valine.

Key Points

  • A nucleotide = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate group.
  • Watson and Crick (1953): DNA is a double helix, 2 nm wide, one turn = 10 base pairs = 3.4 nm.
  • Base pairing is specific: A pairs with T, C pairs with G.
  • A gene is a specific portion of DNA; a change in its base sequence is a mutation.

lessons.notes_html:
RNA is a single polynucleotide chain in which many nucleotides are arranged in a linear sequence. Each nucleotide is made up of three different components: 1. Nitrogenous Bases — Purine (Adenine, Guanine) and Pyrimidine (Cytosine, Uracil); 2. Pentose Sugar (5-Carbon) — Ribose Sugar; 3. Phosphate Group (–PO4). There are four types of nucleotides: Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine and Uracil nucleotides. The RNA is a single stranded, un-branched polynucleotide chain; the single strand is made up of sugar and phosphate in the S – P – S manner, and nitrogenous bases are attached with the sugar.

Types of RNA

  • 1. Messenger RNA (mRNA) — 3–5% of total RNA in a cell. It is formed by DNA inside the nucleus and is the direct complementary copy of DNA. It consists of a single strand of variable length, depending upon the size of the gene: for a protein of 10 amino acids, the mRNA has a length of 30 nucleotides.
  • 2. Transfer RNA (tRNA) — 15% of total RNA. It is also formed by DNA inside the nucleus. It is the smallest RNA, clover shaped, and made up of 73–94 nucleotides.
  • 3. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) — 80% of total RNA. It is also formed by DNA inside the nucleus. It consists of a single strand which coils at many places; in human beings one rRNA consists of about 1800 nucleotides.

Function of RNA

RNA is a carrier of information from DNA. Most plant viruses and some animal viruses have RNA as their genetic material instead of DNA. All three types of RNA are used in the process of protein synthesis: messenger RNA carries the genetic information in the form of codons from DNA to ribosomes; the tRNA brings the amino acids according to the information in the mRNA to form a specific protein molecule — each tRNA picks a specific amino acid from the cytoplasm and takes it to a specific codon on mRNA; the rRNA is associated with the ribosome and helps in the assembly of amino acids in protein molecules.

Protein Synthesis: Transcription and Translation

The process of protein synthesis is the same in all organisms: the information in DNA is converted to information on mRNA, and this information is used to form protein. This whole process is called gene expression or central dogma. It is completed in two main phases:

  • A. Transcription — The process by which information in a strand of DNA is directly copied into an mRNA strand. It occurs inside the nucleus. A specific portion of DNA (gene) that codes for a specific protein opens by the breaking of hydrogen bonds between nitrogenous bases. A single strand of mRNA is formed by pairing the exposed bases on one strand of DNA; the bases on mRNA are complementary to the bases on DNA. After the formation of mRNA, the two strands of DNA recoil to resume their double helical structure, and the newly formed mRNA comes out into the cytoplasm through the nuclear pores.
  • B. Translation — The process in which proteins are formed by using RNA molecules. It occurs in the cytoplasm. The mRNA binds to a ribosome. The information for protein synthesis is present on mRNA in the form of codons (a set of three adjacent bases on mRNA); each codon codes for a specific amino acid. There are about 40–60 different types of tRNA in the cytoplasm. Each transfer RNA has a set of three bases called an anticodon, complementary to a codon on mRNA. After matching its anticodon with a codon on mRNA, the tRNA transfers its amino acid to the mRNA. In this way all amino acids are transferred by tRNA to all the codons on mRNA after matching their anticodons, and the amino acids are linked by peptide bonds. So a specific protein is formed by the information provided by DNA.

Key Points

  • RNA is single stranded, has ribose sugar and uracil instead of thymine.
  • mRNA carries codons, tRNA carries amino acids with anticodons, rRNA builds the ribosome.
  • Central dogma: DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein.

lessons.notes_html:
All organisms are made up of cells, and new cells arise from the division of pre-existing cells. The division of cells is completed after passing through many phases; the specific process of cell division is called the cell cycle. There are two types of cell divisions in living organisms, i.e. mitosis and meiosis. The division of body cells is called mitosis: one diploid cell (2n) divides to form two new diploid daughter cells, and the growth of organisms depends upon it. The division of sex cells is called meiosis: one diploid cell (2n) divides to form four haploid (n) cells called gametes, and sexual reproduction depends upon it.

Cell is the Basic Unit of Life

The organisms may be unicellular or multicellular. The cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of life. The cells of different organisms may be different in shapes and sizes, but structurally all of them are nearly similar. The activities of an organism are the sum of all the activities of the cells present in that organism. Cells having similar functions group together to form tissues. On the basis of structure, cells are of two types:

  • Prokaryotic cell — Lacks a nuclear membrane around the nucleus.
  • Eukaryotic cell — Contains a well developed nuclear membrane.

Animal and Plant Cells

The ultra structure of plant and animal cells shows the same basic plan — cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus with organelles — but plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts and one large central vacuole, while animal cells have centrioles and lysosomes and only small vacuoles.

A plant cell: cell wall, nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplast and a large vacuole.

Key Points

  • The cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of life.
  • Prokaryotic cells have no nuclear membrane; eukaryotic cells have a well developed one.
  • Mitosis divides body cells (2n → 2n); meiosis forms gametes (2n → n).

lessons.notes_html:
An organelle is a sub-cellular structure which has a specific function; it performs one or more functions within the cell. The organelles are of two types: membranous organelles, bounded by a plasma membrane (nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi bodies, mitochondria, lysosomes, plastids, vacuoles), and non-membranous organelles, which have no outer membrane (ribosome, centrioles, cytoskeleton). All the organelles are present in the cytoplasm, which provides the medium for the organelles to carry out their functions.

1. Cell Wall

It is the outermost, hard and non-living covering around the cells of prokaryotes, fungi and plants. In prokaryotes the cell wall is composed of a special compound called peptidoglycan, made up of sugars and amino acids. The cell wall of fungi contains a special compound called chitin. The cell wall of plants usually has two layers: an outer primary wall, mostly composed of cellulose, and an inner secondary wall, thicker than the primary wall and composed of lignin and some other compounds. There are small pores between the cell walls of two adjacent cells called plasmodesmata. The cell wall gives shape to the cell, protects the cell from mechanical damage and infection, and helps in cell-to-cell interaction: the cytoplasmic connection between two adjacent cells through plasmodesmata helps in the transportation of materials among cells.

2. Cell Membrane

The cell membrane or plasma membrane is a thin and elastic membrane, present around the cytoplasm of all prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. In animal cells it is the outermost boundary; in prokaryotes, fungi and plants it is present under the cell wall. The cell membrane consists of a lipid bilayer with embedded proteins; some of these proteins have attached chains of carbohydrates. It is mainly composed of about 60–80% proteins and 20–40% lipids, with small quantities of carbohydrates, though this percentage varies from cell to cell. The cell membrane separates the intracellular components of the cell from the extracellular environment. It acts as a semi permeable barrier: it allows some molecules to pass while preventing the movement of others through it. It controls the transport of materials in (endocytosis) and out (exocytosis) of the cell, and the chemical messages from one cell to another cell are transmitted through the cell membrane. Glycoproteins are special compounds composed of carbohydrates and proteins, while glycolipids are made up of proteins and lipids.

3. Cytoplasm

It is a gelatinous and semi transparent fluid which contains a variety of cell organelles. It is mostly water, and many organic molecules (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids) and inorganic salts are also present in it. It is present between the nucleus and the cell membrane. It acts as a site for various metabolic reactions, e.g. glycolysis, and provides suitable conditions for metabolic reactions. Cytoplasm contains various organelles e.g. ribosomes, Golgi bodies and mitochondria.

4. Cytoskeleton

The cytoskeleton is a network of interconnected filaments and tubules that extend from the nucleus to the plasma membrane in eukaryotic cells. It consists of microtubules, micro filaments and intermediate filaments. Microtubules are involved in cell division and are major components of cilia and flagella. Microfilaments or actin filaments are associated with the shape and structure of the cell. Intermediate filaments help in giving the shape and strength to the cell.

Key Points

  • Cell wall: peptidoglycan in prokaryotes, chitin in fungi, cellulose in plants.
  • Cell membrane is a semi permeable lipid bilayer with 60–80% proteins and 20–40% lipids.
  • Cytoplasm is the site of metabolic reactions like glycolysis; the cytoskeleton gives shape and strength.

5. Nucleus

In 1831, Robert Brown discovered the nucleus in the plant cell. The nucleus is the most prominent organelle within the eukaryotic cell. In animal cells it lies in the centre, but in plant cells it lies on one side due to the presence of a large central vacuole. The nucleus is bounded by a double perforated semi permeable membrane known as the nuclear envelope or nuclear membrane, which separates the nucleus from the cytoplasm. The semifluid content of the nucleus is called nucleoplasm, which contains the nucleolus and chromosomes. The nucleolus is a dark rounded body made up of RNA and protein; it produces ribosomes and ribosomal RNA. The chromosomes are thread-like structures; in a non-dividing cell they are in the form of a network of fine threads called chromatin. The nucleus is called the brain of the cell because it controls the activities of the cell like protein synthesis, metabolism, cell division and growth. It stores hereditary material in the form of DNA.

6. Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)

It is a network of interconnected tiny tube-like structures called cisternae, with cisternal spaces among them. The network of ER is scattered in the cytoplasm from the nuclear envelope to the plasma membrane. The ER is of two types:

  • i) Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER) — The endoplasmic reticulum having many attached ribosomes on its surface. RER is frequently observed in those cells which are actively involved in protein synthesis and secretion.
  • ii) Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER) — The endoplasmic reticulum without attached ribosomes. SER synthesizes the phospholipids present in membranes. In the liver, it helps to detoxify drugs. It is also involved in the transport of large molecules to other parts of the cell.

7. Golgi Apparatus

The Golgi apparatus is named after Camillo Golgi, who discovered it in 1898. It consists of a set of flat and disc shaped sacs called cisternae, present one above the other in a specific manner; the complete set of cisternae is called the Golgi apparatus. It is present in both plants and animals, arranged near the nucleus. In the Golgi complex, the proteins and lipids received from the ER are modified and packed into small membrane bounded sacs called Golgi vesicles. The vesicles which leave the Golgi apparatus move to other parts of the cell; some vesicles proceed to the plasma membrane, where they discharge their contents outside the cell.

Key Points

  • The nucleus (Robert Brown, 1831) is the brain of the cell; its nucleolus makes ribosomes.
  • RER carries ribosomes for protein synthesis; SER makes phospholipids and detoxifies drugs in the liver.
  • The Golgi apparatus (Camillo Golgi, 1898) modifies and packs proteins and lipids into vesicles.

lessons.notes_html:
8. Mitochondria

(Singular: Mitochondrion.) Mitochondria were first discovered by Altmann in 1894. They are filamentous structures surrounded by a double-layered membrane, with a gap between the two membranes. The outer membrane of the mitochondrion has a smooth surface, while the inner membrane forms a number of foldings called cristae, which increase the surface area of the inner membrane. Inside the cristae there is a space filled by a fluid-like material called matrix, which contains many types of chemical compounds, ring-like DNA molecules, RNA molecules and ribosomes. Mitochondria produce cellular energy in the form of ATP, hence they are called the 'power houses' of the cell. They are also called the ATP mill of the cell, the cell furnace or storage batteries, and a semi autonomous organelle.

9. Ribosomes

Ribosomes are granular structures, first observed under the electron microscope by George Palade in 1953. They are formed in the nucleus and are found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells — free in the cytoplasm or attached with the surface of the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The cells of eukaryotes have larger ribosomes than prokaryotes. The ribosomes are composed of equal amounts of RNA and protein. Each ribosome has two sub units, i.e. a smaller unit and a larger unit, and they are not bounded by a membrane. Ribosomes are called the protein factories of the cell because they play a key role in protein synthesis.

10. Centrioles

These are two hollow cylindrical bodies formed by the division of the centrosome. Each centriole is made up of '27' microtubules: there are '9' triplet sets of microtubules, made up of a special protein called tubulin. These organelles are not found in plants; they are clearly visible during the division of animal cells. The centrioles form spindle fibers during cell division, and are also involved in the formation of cilia and flagella in some cells.

11. Lysosomes

Lysosomes are those organelles which are formed by the Golgi apparatus. They were discovered by Christian de Duve in 1949. They are bounded by a single membrane which encloses effective digestive enzymes. The digestive enzymes of lysosomes are capable of digesting various compounds like carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. The lysosomes not only help in intracellular and extracellular digestion but also break down the waste products, and play a very important role in the breakdown of inactive organelles.

Key Points

  • Mitochondria make ATP — the power houses of the cell; their inner folds are cristae.
  • Ribosomes (Palade, 1953) are the protein factories, made of RNA and protein in two subunits.
  • Each centriole has 27 microtubules in 9 triplets; lysosomes (de Duve, 1949) digest wastes and worn-out organelles.

lessons.notes_html:
12. Plastids

These are membrane bounded structures which are found only in plant cells. They usually contain pigments and give plant cells their colours. On the basis of the type of pigments, plastids are classified into chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts.

  • i) Chloroplast — Oval shaped, double membrane structures. There is a space between the two membranes, and the cavity of the chloroplast is filled with a liquid material called stroma. The outer membrane is smooth while the inner membrane forms sac-like structures called thylakoids. Thylakoids are arranged in stacks like the piles of coins, called grana (singular: granum). They contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which captures sunlight for photosynthesis. Thylakoids also have small circular DNA and ribosomes.
  • ii) Chromoplasts — These organelles contain coloured pigments other than chlorophyll. The yellow, red or orange colours in plants are due to chromoplasts. They are present in the petals of flowers: due to the bright colours of chromoplasts in petals, insects are attracted towards flowers for pollination. Chromoplasts are also found in ripened fruits and vegetables, e.g. the red colour of an apple and tomato is due to chromoplasts.
  • iii) Leucoplasts — The colourless plastids of varied shapes and sizes, with stored nutrients. They are usually found in underground parts of the plant and store food, e.g. potato stores starch.

13. Vacuoles

These are sac-like organelles in the cytoplasm of both plant and animal cells. They are small in size but large in number in animal cells. In plant cells there is a central large vacuole which pushes the nucleus at a side. Each vacuole is bounded by a single membrane called tonoplast. In plant cells, the tonoplast of the central large vacuole encloses a solution of different salts, sugar and amino acids etc. In animal cells there are usually two types of vacuoles, i.e. food vacuole and contractile vacuole: the food is brought inside the cell by the food vacuole, while the contractile vacuole is for osmoregulation, i.e. regulation of water — Amoeba has both these types of vacuoles.

Structural Advantages of Plant and Animal Cells

The differences in the structure of plant and animal cells are actually their adaptations, necessary for their mode of lives. Plants are autotrophic and sessile; animals are heterotrophic and mobile, facing different environments like forest and desert.

  • Plants — Cell Wall: gives shape to the plant cell; plasmodesmata maintain the cytoplasmic connection between adjacent cells; cell walls give plant stems and wood their stiffness, limit the entry of large molecules that may be toxic, act as pressure vessels when water enters xylem vessels, and protect from mechanical injury and infections.
  • Plants — Chloroplast: absorbs sunlight and uses it to form food (glucose) with the help of water and CO2 by photosynthesis. Life on earth directly or indirectly depends upon plants; chloroplasts absorb CO2 from the air and release O2 into the atmosphere for respiration.
  • Plants — Vacuole: the central large vacuole is filled with cell sap, which stores nutrients, maintains turgor pressure and gives support to the cell.
  • Animals — Cell Membrane: animal cells have no cell walls; their outermost covering is the thin, flexible and porous cell membrane, which provides more flexibility in shape, helps in locomotion, and transports materials in and out of the cell.
  • Animals — Lysosomes: present in all animal cells and absent in plant cells; they contain many digestive enzymes, help in intracellular digestion and remove waste materials from the cell.
  • Animals — Vacuoles: many small vacuoles perform functions like storage and transport of different substances.

Key Points

  • Plastids occur only in plant cells: chloroplasts (green), chromoplasts (coloured), leucoplasts (colourless, store food).
  • The vacuole membrane is the tonoplast; animal cells have food and contractile vacuoles.
  • Plant and animal cell differences are adaptations to their way of life.

lessons.notes_html:
All the cells of organisms have nearly the same structure, but the cells of different organisms or of organs within the same body have different shapes, sizes and functions.

Different Types of Cells

  • A) Epidermal Cells and Mesophyll Cells — Leaves are the photosynthetic organs of plants, made up of various specialized tissues. The epidermis is the outermost layer of single cells on both the upper and lower leaf surfaces. There are many tiny pores in the epidermis called stomata; each stoma is surrounded by two bean shaped cells called guard cells that contain chlorophyll. The guard cells regulate the opening and closing of stomata to control transpiration. The epidermis is covered by a waxy cuticle, which prevents water loss and stops the entry of pathogens and unwanted substances into the leaf. The tissues between the upper and lower epidermis are called mesophyll tissues, of two types: palisade mesophyll cells are column shaped, tightly packed and located just below the upper epidermis; they contain a lot of chloroplasts and are mainly responsible for most of the photosynthesis in the leaf. The spongy mesophyll cells are round, loosely packed and located below the palisade layer; they carry out less photosynthesis in the leaf.
  • B) Neurons — The neurons or nerve cells are the structural and functional units of the animal's nervous system. These are the longest cells in the animal's body. A typical neuron consists of three main parts: the cell body is the main part of the neuron; dendrites are the branches that arise from the cell body and carry impulses towards the cell body; the axon is a single and long branch arising from the cell body and carries impulses away from the cell body.
  • C) Muscle Cell — A muscle is a bundle of thousands of long cylindrical muscle fibers enclosed in a sheath of connective tissue. The muscles are mainly composed of two types of proteins, i.e. actin and myosin. There are three types of muscles: cardiac muscle (in heart), skeletal muscle (with bones) and smooth muscle (in blood vessels and digestive tract).
  • D) Red Blood Cells (RBC) — RBCs (Erythrocytes) are a component of blood, made in the bone marrow. Each RBC is small, round and a biconcave body bounded by a membrane. Its red colour is due to a red protein called haemoglobin. The life of an RBC is about 120 days. Its main function is to carry oxygen from the lungs to every cell of the body.
  • E) Liver Cell — Each liver cell is a round shaped cell enclosed by a membrane, with a central nucleus and cytoplasm having a large number of organelles with metabolic and secretory functions. The liver cell is also called a hepatocyte, and the liver is called the chemical factory of the body.

Division of Labour

According to cell theory, the activities of an organism are the sum total of all the activities of cells present in that organism. There is a division of labour within the cell and across the cells. Within a cell: ribosomes are the protein factories; the Golgi complex modifies and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles for transport; mitochondria produce cellular energy in the form of ATP and are called power houses; SER synthesizes phospholipids and detoxifies drugs, especially in the liver; RER is involved in protein synthesis and secretion; lysosomes contain enzymes that digest macromolecules and wastes and break down old organelles; vacuoles store many substances and remove wastes; centrioles help in cell division and formation of cilia/flagella; the nucleus controls cell activities like protein synthesis, metabolism and growth, so it is called the brain of the cell, and chromosomes and genes are found in the nucleus; plastids are found only in plant cells and are the site of photosynthesis. Across cells: tissues are groups of similar cells that perform a specific function, for example the contraction of muscle tissue occurs due to the combined action of muscle fibers; organs are made up of different tissues working together, for example the stomach is made up of smooth muscles, glandular muscles and connective tissues; organ systems are formed by organs having related functions, for example the digestive system consists of mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. All organ systems in a body work interdependently and in coordination to maintain the functions of the body.

Cell Specialization

It is a process in which cells with specific structures and functions are formed by unspecialized cells called stem cells. Cell specialization is vital for the survival and functions of multicellular organisms. It starts during embryonic development: in the embryo there are stem cells, which are not specialized and can become any type of cell. These cells form different organs of the body, and each organ performs a specific function. A male gamete and a female gamete unite to form a zygote, which divides many times to form the embryo.

Key Points

  • Specialized cells: epidermal and mesophyll cells in leaves, neurons, muscle cells, RBCs (120-day life) and liver cells (hepatocytes).
  • Division of labour works within a cell (organelles) and across cells (tissues, organs, organ systems).
  • Stem cells are unspecialized cells that form all specialized cell types.

lessons.notes_html:
The cell division cycle or cell cycle is a process by which a parent cell divides into daughter cells; it is a series of events. These events are divided into two main phases, i.e. interphase and division phase. An interphase is a preparatory phase of the cell cycle in which the metabolic activities of parent cells are at their peak. In the division phase, the parent cells divide into daughter cells. There are two types of cell division, i.e. mitosis and meiosis: in mitosis a parent cell divides into two daughter cells; in meiosis, a parent cell first divides into two daughter cells and each daughter cell further divides into two cells. The time taken by a cell cycle is variable: in yeast (fungus) mitosis is completed in about 90 minutes, while it takes about 24 hours in human beings.

Phases of the Cell Cycle

  • A. Interphase — Commonly considered the resting phase between two successive mitotic phases, but in actual practice it is the time during which the cell is preparing for division by undergoing both cell growth and DNA replication. The interphase takes about 90% of the total duration of the cell cycle. It is further divided into three phases: i) G1 Phase (Gap 1) — the interval between mitosis and the initiation of DNA replication; during G1 phase the cell is metabolically active and continuously grows in size and increases the number of its organelles. ii) S Phase (Synthesis) — the period during which DNA synthesis or replication takes place in the nucleus, i.e. each chromosome duplicates into two sister chromatids. iii) G2 Phase (Gap 2) — proteins are synthesised for the production of spindle fibres, and the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm.
  • B. Division Phase (M Phase) — Starts with nuclear division, corresponding to the separation of daughter chromosomes (karyokinesis), and usually ends with the division of cytoplasm (cytokinesis). Some cells in adult animals do not undergo cell division (e.g. heart cells), and many other cells divide only occasionally, as needed to replace cells lost because of injury or cell death. Cells that do not divide further exit the G1 phase to enter an inactive stage called the quiescent stage (G0) of the cell cycle; cells in this stage remain metabolically active but no longer multiply.

Mitosis

Mitosis was first observed by a German biologist Walther Flemming in 1882. In this division, the parent somatic cell (body cell) divides into two daughter cells in which the number of chromosomes remains the same as in the parent cell. The process of mitosis is divided into two main phases, i.e. karyokinesis (nuclear division) and cytokinesis (cytoplasmic division).

A. Karyokinesis — Four Stages

  • i) Prophase — The first stage of mitosis after interphase. The chromatin network condenses to form chromosomes, seen to be composed of two sister chromatids attached together at the centromere; the centromere has a protein structure called the kinetochore where the spindle fibres get attached. The centrioles move towards opposite poles of the cell and start to form spindle fibres. The nucleolus and nuclear membrane degrade and disappear.
  • ii) Metaphase — The spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores of chromosomes, called kinetochore fibres; a number of non-kinetochore fibres from opposite centrioles attach with each other. Two kinetochore fibers from opposite poles attach with each chromosome. The chromosomes are moved to the spindle equator and get arranged along the metaphase plate — the plane of alignment of the chromosomes on the equator. The fibers which attach with kinetochores are called kinetochore spindle fibers, while others are called non-kinetochore spindle fibers.
  • iii) Anaphase — The kinetochore spindle fibres contract and are pulled towards the centrioles. Due to the pulling force, centromeres split and sister chromatids separate; these sister chromatids are now called sister chromosomes. The chromosomes are pulled towards the opposite poles.
  • iv) Telophase — Chromosomes reach the opposite poles and again unfold as chromatin. Nuclear envelopes reappear around the two chromosome clusters. Nucleolus, Golgi complex and endoplasmic reticulum are reformed.

B. Cytokinesis

It is the physical process of cell division which divides the cytoplasm of the parent cell into two daughter cells. In an animal cell, this is achieved by the appearance of a cleavage furrow in the plasma membrane; the furrow gradually deepens and ultimately joins in the centre, dividing the cell into two cells. Plant cells are enclosed by cell walls, so cytokinesis occurs by a different mechanism: vesicles of Golgi bodies are collected in the middle of the plant cell and fuse to form a membranous structure called the cell plate or phragmoplast. The cell plate grows outwards and finally fuses with the plasma membrane and parent cell wall; in this way two daughter plant cells are formed. At the time of cytokinesis, the cell organelles like mitochondria and plastids get distributed between the two daughter cells.

Significance of Mitosis

  • Mitosis results in the production of diploid daughter cells with identical number of chromosomes.
  • The growth of multicellular organisms is due to mitosis of a single cell (zygote).
  • A very significant contribution of mitosis is cell repair and replacement of old cells by new ones.
  • The cells of the upper layer of the epidermis, cells of the lining of the gut, and blood cells are being constantly replaced by mitosis.
  • Mitotic divisions in the meristem tissues, the apical and the lateral meristem, result in a continuous growth of plants throughout their life.
  • Regeneration of the lost parts of the body in many organisms takes place by mitosis, e.g. arms of star fish.

Key Points

  • Cell cycle = interphase (G1, S, G2; about 90% of the time) + division phase; non-dividing cells rest in G0.
  • Mitosis (Flemming, 1882): prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis.
  • Animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow; plant cells by a cell plate (phragmoplast).

lessons.notes_html:
Meiosis is the process by which one diploid (2n) cell divides to form four haploid (n) daughter cells. It was discovered in 1876 by a German biologist Oscar Hertwig. Meiosis takes place in plants and animals and ultimately leads to the formation of haploid gametes. The process starts from interphase, which includes G1, S and G2 phases; after interphase, two successive phases start, i.e. meiosis-I and meiosis-II.

Meiosis-I

  • a) Prophase-I — A complex and longest phase of meiosis. i) The chromatin material is condensed and appears in the form of chromosomes. ii) The homologous chromosomes come close to each other and form pairs; this process is called synapsis. Each pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes is called a bivalent, and each bivalent has four chromatids, so it is called a tetrad. iii) In a homologous chromosome pair, the non-sister chromatids attach lengthwise with each other at some places, called chiasmata. iv) The non-sister chromatids exchange their segments at chiasmata; this process is called crossing over, and due to it there is an exchange of genetic information between the homologous chromosomes. v) After crossing over, the chromosomes become more thick due to further condensation. vi) The nuclear membrane breaks and nucleoli are disappeared. vii) Two centrioles migrate to the opposite poles of the cell and form spindle fibers. (Homologous chromosomes are a chromosome pair in a diploid cell: they have similar shape and size and the same genes at the same locations (loci).)
  • b) Metaphase-I — The dispersed bivalents in the cytoplasm arrange themselves in the center of the cell, called the equator; a metaphase plate is formed in the middle of the cell. The kinetochore fibers of each side attach with the bivalent of its own side.
  • c) Anaphase-I — Due to the contraction of kinetochore spindle fibers, the two homologous chromosomes of a bivalent separate from each other and move towards the respective poles. In this phase the centromere does not break.
  • d) Telophase-I — Half the number of chromosomes reach at one pole and half at the opposite pole, so two haploid sets of chromosomes are formed in the cell. The spindle fibers disappear, nucleoli reappear, the nuclear membrane reappears around each haploid set of chromosomes, and the chromosomes uncoil into chromatin material again.
  • B. Cytokinesis — A cleavage furrow is formed in the middle of the cell membrane by the division of cytoplasm, dividing the cell into two daughter cells. In plant cells, cytokinesis occurs due to the formation of a cell plate.

Interphase-II is a brief period of time between two meiotic divisions (Meiosis-I and Meiosis-II), also called interkinesis. It is different from the interphase-I of meiosis because it has no S-phase, so no duplication of chromosomes occurs in meiosis-II.

Meiosis-II

Meiosis-II is like normal mitosis and also has four phases: a) Prophase-II — the chromatin material is condensed to form chromosomes; nuclear membrane and nucleoli disappear; the centrioles on opposite poles of the cell form spindle fibers. b) Metaphase-II — the chromosomes align at the equator and the spindle fibres from opposite poles of the spindle get attached to the kinetochores of sister chromatids. c) Anaphase-II — due to the contraction of kinetochore spindle fibers, a pulling force is applied on the centromere; the centromere breaks due to this force and sister chromatids are separated from each other and move towards opposite poles of the cell. d) Telophase-II — meiosis ends with telophase II, in which the two sets of chromosomes once again get enclosed by a nuclear envelope. After telophase-II, cytokinesis starts, due to which four daughter haploid gametes are formed.

Comparison of Mitosis and Meiosis

MitosisMeiosis
It occurs in all somatic cells for growth.It occurs only in gonads or germline cells for the formation of gametes.
The whole process completes in one division.The process completes in two divisions.
Prophase is of short duration.Prophase-I is of longer duration.
Crossing over does not occur. Chiasmata is not formed.Crossing over takes place with the formation of chiasmata.
Centromeres divide in metaphase.Centromere do not divide (in meiosis-I).
All chromosomes behave independently and no pairing of chromosomes occurs.Homologous chromosomes pair and form bivalents by synapsis.
2 daughter cells are formed.4 daughter cells are formed.

Significance of Meiosis

  • Due to meiosis, haploid gametes (n) are formed, which are the main units for sexual reproduction. By the union of male and female haploid gametes, the diploid number (2n) is restored in the next generation, so the number of chromosomes of a particular species remains constant generation after generation.
  • Due to crossing over, new combinations of genes are formed on chromosomes, due to which variations occur in the new generation. Variations are very important for the process of evolution.

Stem Cells as Unspecialized Cells

Stem cells are master cells in the body having the unique ability to renew themselves and to differentiate into many different types of specialized cells in the body. They are found in the embryo of organisms. They have no specific functions like other specialized cells; they are immature and unspecialized cells, but have the ability to grow into any type of specialized cells, through a process called differentiation. Stem cells differ from other specialized cells: i) they can divide and renew themselves over a long time; ii) they are unspecialized because they do not have tissue specific structures; iii) they have the potential to become specialized cells; iv) they do not have special morphology. Examples: in plants, stem cells are found close to the tips of shoot and roots and are called meristems — branches, leaves, flowers and roots are formed from these meristems. The embryonic stem cells in the human body are the most potent, because every type of cell in the body is derived from them, for example blood cells, brain cells, muscle cells and bone cells.

Key Points

  • Meiosis (Hertwig, 1876): one diploid cell → four haploid gametes, in two divisions.
  • Prophase-I is the longest phase: synapsis forms bivalents, and crossing over exchanges segments at chiasmata.
  • Meiosis keeps the chromosome number constant across generations and creates variation.
  • Stem cells are unspecialized master cells; in plants they are the meristems.

lessons.notes_html:
We know that the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of the body of all organisms. A group of similar cells having similar functions is called tissue. A group of two or more types of tissue that work together to complete a specific function is called an organ. A group of organs having related functions that work together to perform a specific function is called an organ system. An individual or organism is formed by the organization of different organ systems. In this chapter we study the levels of organization in organisms, from cellular level to organism level, the organs and organ systems involved in homeostasis, disorders of organs and organ systems in animals, and the structure and roles of various plant organs in plant physiology.

Tissues, Organs and Systems

A group of similar cells that work together to perform a specific function is called tissue; for example, muscle is a tissue made up of muscle fibers, and all muscle fibers work together so movement occurs. There are many types of cells in the epidermis of a leaf, and all these cells work together as a tissue. An organ is a self contained part of the body that performs a specific function or functions. In the body, organs are made up of tissues that work together for a common purpose; for example, the stomach is an organ made up of different tissues like smooth muscles and glandular tissues. A leaf is an organ because it is made up of different types of tissues, i.e. epidermal, spongy mesophyll and palisade mesophyll. An organ system is a group of different organs having related functions that work together to perform a complex function in the body; for example, the digestion process is completed by the digestive system, made up of different organs like esophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. The pineal gland is the smallest organ while the skin is the largest organ of the human body.

Levels of Organization

Levels of organization are also called the hierarchy of life. Each upper level of organization will be more complex as compared to the lower one: atoms combine to form molecules; molecules combine to form organelles; different organelles combine to form a cell; cells combine to form tissues; different tissues combine to form an organ; different organs combine to form an organ system, and different organ systems combine to form the body of an individual.

  • A. Cell Organelles and Cell — The living subcellular structures in a cell are called cell organelles, formed by the specific combination of biomolecules. The division of work inside a cell is carried out by these organelles; each organelle performs a specific function in a cell, for example ribosomes are specialized for protein synthesis. Different cell organelles collectively form the cell. All organisms are made up of cells, which have different shapes, sizes and functions. On the basis of the number of cells, organisms are of two types: i) Unicellular (made up of a single cell), for example amoeba, chlamydomonas and paramecium; ii) Multi-cellular (made up of many cells), for example the human body, which consists of more than 37.2 trillion cells.
  • B. Tissue — A group of cells having similar structure and function. Multicellular organisms have different types of tissues. Each cell in a tissue carries on its own life processes, e.g. protein synthesis and ATP production; a cell also carries on some special processes related to the function of the tissue. Muscular and nervous tissues are animal tissues, while xylem and epidermal tissues are plant tissues.
  • C. Organ — A group of different tissues having related functions. Each organ performs a specific function, and the functions of its tissues collectively become the function of that organ. For example, the human stomach is an organ whose function is to digest food: two types of tissues are involved in the digestion of food in the stomach — the secretory tissues secrete gastric juice for the digestion of food, while the muscular tissues contract the wall of the stomach for crushing and mixing of the food with gastric juice. The heart is the first organ that forms during the development of the body.
  • D. Organ System — A group of organs having related functions. Each organ carries out its specific function, and all the functions of these organs become the function of that system; for example, the digestive system consists of mouth, stomach, small intestine and large intestine.
  • Organism Level — An individual or organism is formed by the organization of different organ systems, for example the human being, made up of different systems such as the circulatory system, respiratory system and digestive system. There is a coordination between different organs and organ systems of an individual: for example, during playing, our muscles work; for the extra working of muscles there is a need of more food and oxygen to the muscles. This supply is brought about by the increased flow of blood to muscles, controlled by the increased heart beat. More oxygen is supplied by the lungs to the blood. More CO2 is produced during playing, so there is an increase in the rate of respiration to get more oxygen and to remove more CO2. More heat is produced in our body during playing, due to which body temperature increases; to maintain the body temperature, our sweat glands produce sweat from our skin.

Key Points

  • Hierarchy of life: atoms → molecules → organelles → cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
  • The human body has more than 37.2 trillion cells; the skin is its largest organ and the pineal gland the smallest.
  • Organ systems work in coordination, as seen when the body plays and sweats.

lessons.notes_html:
Composition of Stomach on Tissue Level

The stomach is a J-shaped muscular sac, present beneath the diaphragm. In an adult person, the stomach is nearly 12 inches long and 6 inches wide. The following tissues combine to form the stomach:

  • A. Smooth Muscles — These muscles in the wall of the stomach are present in the form of layers. The innermost layer is called mucosa. The second layer is called sub-mucosa, the third layer is called muscularis and the outermost layer of muscles is called serosa.
  • B. Glandular Tissues — The mucosa has gastric glands composed of three kinds of cells: 1. Chief cells secrete an inactive enzyme called pepsinogen, which is converted into an active enzyme pepsin by HCl. Pepsin acts on protein and converts it into partially digested polypeptides and amino acids. 2. Parietal cells secrete HCl; it softens the food and kills pathogens in food. 3. Mucous cells secrete mucous, which forms a coating on the inner walls of the stomach, so the walls of the stomach become safe from the action of HCl and pepsin.
  • C. Blood Capillaries — Blood capillaries are also part of the stomach, and the walls of blood capillaries are also made of tissues.

Composition of a Leaf on Tissue Level

Leaves are called the photosynthetic organs of plants. Each leaf is made up of different types of tissues, and the cells of the leaf system have a variety of specialized structures and functions. The outermost covering of a leaf is called epidermis, composed of a single layer of cells forming the upper and lower surfaces of a leaf, called upper and lower epidermis respectively. There are many tiny pores in the epidermis called stomata. Around each stoma there are two bean shaped cells called guard cells. The guard cells are responsible for the opening and closing of stomata to control transpiration. The epidermis is covered by a waxy layer of cuticle, which prevents the loss of water from the leaf and stops the entry of pathogens and unwanted substances into the leaf. The tissues between the upper and lower epidermis are called mesophyll tissues, of two types: the palisade mesophyll cells are column shaped, closely packed and present just below the upper epidermis; these cells contain a lot of chloroplasts, so they are responsible for most of the photosynthesis in the leaf. The spongy mesophyll cells are rounded in shape, loosely packed and present beneath the palisade tissues; there are air spaces among spongy mesophyll cells which allow the removal of oxygen and entry of CO2 into the leaf. There is less chloroplast in spongy mesophyll than palisade mesophyll cells, so there is less photosynthesis in the spongy mesophyll layer. In the leaves there is a central vessel called midrib, and many branches arise from the midrib called leaf veins. The midrib and veins contain xylem for the transportation of water and phloem for the transportation of food. Leaves look green because, when sunlight falls on plants, the green portion of light is reflected by the chlorophyll.

Key Points

  • Stomach wall layers: mucosa, sub-mucosa, muscularis, serosa; its glands have chief, parietal and mucous cells.
  • Pepsinogen is activated to pepsin by HCl; mucous protects the stomach wall from both.
  • A leaf is an organ of epidermal, palisade and spongy mesophyll tissues, with xylem and phloem in its veins.

lessons.notes_html:
The human body is made up of different organ systems.

1. Digestive System

Food is digested by the digestive system and the undigested material is removed from the body. The human digestive system is in the form of a tract which starts from the mouth and ends at the anus. This system consists of mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. The length of the small intestine in an adult human is about 6–7 m, while the length of the large intestine is about 1.5 m.

2. Respiratory System

It is the system of gaseous exchange. Oxygen is taken inside the body, where the breakdown of glucose is carried out; by this breakdown, CO2 and energy (ATP) are produced. ATP is used inside the body while CO2 is removed from the body. The respiratory system consists of nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and lungs.

3. Cardiovascular System

It is the system of blood circulation in the body. Blood supplies O2 and food to all parts of the body; in the same way, blood carries CO2 and waste materials from different organs and carries these materials to excretory organs to remove them from the body. The circulatory system consists of heart, blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) and blood. The size of the human heart is equal to the closed fist of the person.

4. Reproductive System

The reproductive system of male and female is different. Both the systems produce gametes: male gametes (sperms) and female gametes (eggs). The sperm and egg unite to form a zygote. The zygote divides many times to form an embryo, and from the embryo a new baby is formed inside the body of the mother.

5. Nervous System

The nervous system is the complex network of cells and fibers in the body. It is divided into two parts, i.e. the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS includes the brain and spinal cord. The PNS consists of those nerves which arise from the brain and spinal cord; it connects the CNS to the rest of the body nerves. The nervous system is the control center of the body: it controls and coordinates all body activities, for example heart beat, respiration and movement.

6. Endocrine System

It is a system of some special glands called ductless glands or endocrine glands, for example the pituitary gland and thyroid gland. These glands produce special compounds called hormones, which are directly added into the blood. The hormones play very important roles in the proper functioning of the human body; the deficiency or over production of hormones causes serious problems and even death. Key Points
