lessons.notes_html:
When an organ does not function properly it is called an organ disorder. Some examples of organ disorders are as follows:

A. Ulcer

It is a disorder of the inner wall of the stomach and the first part of the small intestine (duodenum). When there is improper coating of mucous on the inner wall of the stomach or gut, then the HCl and pepsin in the gastric juice destroy the tissue of the inner walls, causing a wound. This wound is called a peptic ulcer or ulcer. The ulcer of the stomach is called gastric ulcer, while the ulcer of the duodenum is called duodenal ulcer. Pain in the stomach after a meal is the common symptom of ulcer; severe pain, loss of appetite and nausea are the signs of chronic ulcer. There could be many reasons of ulcer, such as Helicobacter pylori infection, excess of HCl or pepsin in the stomach, excessive intake of spicy food, coffee and carbonated drinks, excessive smoking, and prolong use of pain killer medicines. Ulcer can be prevented by avoiding smoking, excessive intake of spicy food and carbonated drinks, and over use of medicines. Antacid medicines neutralize the acidic effects of gastric juice, and ulcer caused by bacteria is treated with antibiotics.

B. Heart Attack (Myocardial Infarction)

The term "myocardial infarction" is composed of two Greek words: 'Myocardial' means heart muscles and 'Infarction' means tissue death. Myocardial infarction is the general term used for damage or death of heart muscles; it is commonly known as heart attack. The causing factors are plaque and thrombus formation in the coronary arteries. The factors leading to myocardial infarction are obesity, metabolic syndrome and chronic kidney disease. The potential triggering factors are excessive physical activity, excessive alcohol intake and drug addiction. The most common symptom is severe chest pain or discomfort; the pain travels most often to the left arm, and may also travel to the neck, lower jaw and back, with difficulty in breathing, unconsciousness, anxiety and nausea. The treatment involves angioplasty and heart bypass surgery. The preventive measures include change in life style, exercise, patient and family education, control of hypertension, no smoking, weight management and medication prescribed according to the need of the patient.

C. Pneumonia

It is a respiratory tract disorder and a serious disorder of the lungs. In this case inflammation occurs in the walls of air sacs (alveoli) and there is accumulation of fluid and pus in the air sacs of the lungs. Pneumonia is caused by bacteria, virus or fungi. The common symptoms are chest pain, cough, chills, fever, muscle pain and red brown sputum. Pneumonia can be treated by antibiotics.

D. Brain Tumor

It is a disorder of the nervous system. In this case an abnormal mass of brain cells is produced as a result of uncontrolled cell division. The tumor may be benign or malignant. The tumor is caused by mutation; it may occur in any age in the brain and spinal cord. The common symptoms of tumor are headache, vision problem, hearing problems, seizures and coma. The tumor is removed surgically.

E. Goiter

It is a disorder of the endocrine glands. In this case the thyroid gland becomes enlarged due to the deficiency of iodine. The primary symptom of goiter is a visible swelling in the front of the neck. Other symptoms are increased heart rate, increase in sweating, increase in body weight and weak nails. The thyroid can be treated by proper medicines or may be removed surgically.

Key Points

  • Ulcer: HCl and pepsin wound the stomach or duodenum wall when the mucous coating fails; H. pylori is a main cause.
  • Heart attack (myocardial infarction) is death of heart muscle from blocked coronary arteries.
  • Pneumonia fills the alveoli with fluid and pus; brain tumor comes from uncontrolled cell division; goiter from iodine deficiency.

lessons.notes_html:
Homeostasis is a process by which living organisms keep their internal environment stable and balanced. The main aspects of homeostasis are osmoregulation (balance of water and salts in the body), excretion (removal of wastes) and thermoregulation (maintenance of constant body temperature). Humans possess a highly developed system for homeostasis; the main homeostatic organs are lungs, skin and kidneys.

A. Lungs as Homeostatic Organ

During cellular respiration, CO2 is produced due to the breakdown of organic substances from cells, which diffuses into the blood via tissue fluid. CO2 is an acidic gas which decreases the pH of blood and makes it acidic (the normal pH of blood is 7.3 to 7.4). This results in the disturbance of many chemical reactions in our body, therefore it should be removed immediately. Blood transports CO2 from tissue fluid to lungs for its removal through the respiratory passage.

B. Skin as Homeostatic Organ

Our skin produces sweat through sweat glands, which contains water, salts and a small quantity of urea. Skin also performs an important role in thermoregulation. The skin consists of epidermis (outer layer of skin) and dermis. There is a thin layer of fat cells (adipose tissue) around and beneath the dermis, which acts as an insulator. The sensory nerve endings in skin are stimulated by cold and warm temperature. The contraction of small erectile muscles, which are attached to hair, forms "goose bumps" (i.e. hair erected): it creates an insulating blanket and prevents heat loss from the body. Similarly, when the body becomes overheated, the hair erectile muscles relax to remove extra heat. Excess heat is also removed through the evaporation of sweat.

C. Kidneys as Homeostatic Organs

Kidneys are major excretory and osmoregulatory organs in humans. They remove nitrogen containing wastes (like urea, uric acid, ammonia, creatinine etc.), drugs, used hormones, excess salts and toxic substances. Kidneys maintain water balance in the body either by absorbing or removing water. They also help in the maintenance of blood and lymph composition and volume. The liver also helps in homeostasis: it regulates the levels of hepatic glucose, breaks down the dead RBCs and removes bilirubin (waste of broken RBCs).

Advantages of Homeostasis

Homeostasis is a very important phenomenon in living organisms; the life of an organism is not possible without homeostasis. It keeps the balance of water and salts in the body. Due to homeostasis the waste products are removed from the body. Homeostasis keeps the body environment under control and keeps the conditions favourable for cells to function. If homeostasis does not maintain properly, then processes inside the body will not function properly.

Key Points

  • Homeostasis = osmoregulation + excretion + thermoregulation.
  • Lungs remove CO2 to keep blood pH at 7.3–7.4; skin sweats and raises goose bumps; kidneys remove nitrogenous wastes and balance water.
  • The liver regulates glucose and removes bilirubin from dead RBCs.

lessons.notes_html:
Plant physiology is concerned with all those processes which occur within the plant body. In a simple way, we can say that plant physiology is a combined action of root, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds.

  • 1. Root — It is the underground part of the plant. Roots perform many functions: they anchor the plant firmly in the soil, and absorb water and minerals by root hairs.
  • 2. Stem — The stem or shoot is the above ground part of the plant. Inside the stem there are xylem and phloem tissues. Water and minerals are transported to all parts of the plant body by xylem. The phloem transports food from the leaves to all parts of the plant.
  • 3. Leaves — A green leaf is called the kitchen of the plant because photosynthesis occurs here and, as a result, glucose is formed. The extra water is removed from the leaves in the form of vapours; this process is called transpiration. The exchange of gases (CO2, O2) also occurs through the stomata of leaves.
  • 4. Flower — It is the reproductive part of the plant. The bright colours of flowers attract insects for pollination. Male gametes (sperms) are formed in the anther of the stamen and female gametes (eggs) are formed in the ovaries of the carpel. Sperm and egg unite to form a zygote by the process of fertilization. The zygote divides repeatedly to form an embryo, and from the embryo a new plant is formed.
  • 5. Fruit — The ripened ovary with seeds is called fruit. Fruit is a store house of nutrients.
  • 6. Seeds — New plants are formed by the development of the embryo present inside the seed, by the process called seed germination.

Key Points

  • Roots anchor and absorb; the stem transports (xylem up, phloem for food); leaves are the kitchen of the plant.
  • The flower reproduces, the fruit is the ripened ovary, and the seed grows into a new plant by germination.

lessons.notes_html:
Bioenergetics is the quantitative study of energy transformations that accompany biochemical reactions; it is a branch of biology that deals with the energy budget of living systems. We already know that within the cell different processes occur, some of them require energy (endergonic reactions) while others release energy (exergonic reactions). Thus there is a continuous flow of energy within the cell.

Metabolism

Metabolism is the set of chemical reactions which occur in the body for the maintenance of life. The term "metabolism" was derived from the Greek word "metabole", which means "to change". Metabolism has two parts:

  • i) Anabolism (Synthetic or Building Process) — It is the constructive phase of metabolism in which larger molecules are formed from smaller molecules. For example, when amino acids join with each other to form protein, it is an anabolic reaction.
  • ii) Catabolism (Degradative or Breaking Process) — It is the destructive phase of metabolism in which larger molecules are converted into smaller molecules. For example, when protein breaks down to form amino acids, it is a catabolic reaction.

Metabolic reactions in which energy is released are called catabolic reactions, while reactions in which energy is required are called anabolic reactions. The energy released in catabolic reactions is used in anabolic reactions; in this way metabolism maintains the energy balance in the body.

Key Points

  • Metabolism (metabole = to change) is the set of life-maintaining chemical reactions.
  • Anabolism builds large molecules from small ones (needs energy); catabolism breaks them down (releases energy).

lessons.notes_html:
Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions by lowering the activation energy. The reactions of digestion in our body complete in 3–4 hours with the help of enzymes (pepsin, maltase, lipase). Let us learn the mechanism of enzyme action, the factors affecting enzyme action, and some enzyme inhibitors.

Characteristics of Enzymes

  • i) All enzymes are proteins in nature.
  • ii) Enzymes are used in very small amounts and are highly efficient; they remain unaffected after the reaction.
  • iii) They are highly specific in their actions; one enzyme can catalyze only one specific reaction.
  • iv) They are reversible in nature, because they can catalyze both forward and reverse reactions.
  • v) Enzymes require an optimum temperature and pH for maximum activity.
  • vi) They are thermolabile in nature: they can be destroyed by heat.
  • vii) Enzymes reduce the activation energy of chemical reactions (the minimum energy needed for the reactants to start the reaction).
  • viii) Enzymes can work repeatedly because they are not consumed in the chemical reaction.
  • ix) Enzymes may need co-factors for proper working.
  • x) The activity of enzymes can be decreased or blocked by inhibitors.
  • xi) Some enzymes are produced in an inactive form, called zymogens (pro-enzymes), and they become active when needed.
  • xii) The molecular weight of enzymes is very high.

Mechanism of Action of Enzymes

The enzyme and substrate combine to form an Enzyme-Substrate (ES) complex; the ES complex then changes into the Enzyme-Product (EP) complex, and finally the product is released while the enzyme remains unchanged. Two models explain enzyme action:

  • i) Lock and Key Model — It was given by Fischer in 1894. According to this model, the active site of the enzyme is rigid and only a specific substrate fits in it, just like a specific key fits in a specific lock. When a specific substrate molecule fits in the active site of an enzyme, the ES complex is formed and finally changed into product.
  • ii) Induced Fit Model — It was given by Koshland in 1958. According to this model, the active site of the enzyme is not rigid but flexible; when the substrate comes close to the active site of the enzyme, the active site changes its shape and fits exactly around the substrate. It is like a hand fitting into a glove.

Enzyme + substrate → ES complex → products, and the enzyme is free to work again.

Key Points

  • Enzymes are specific, reversible, thermolabile proteins that lower activation energy and stay unchanged.
  • Lock and key model: Fischer, 1894. Induced fit model: Koshland, 1958 — the active site adjusts its shape.

lessons.notes_html:
Factors Affecting Enzyme Action

  • i) Enzyme Concentration — The rate of an enzymatic reaction is directly proportional to the concentration of enzyme: if enzyme concentration is increased, the rate of the reaction is increased up to a saturation point (beyond which there is no increase in the rate of reaction).
  • ii) Substrate Concentration — The rate of an enzymatic reaction is directly proportional to the concentration of substrate: if substrate concentration increases, the rate of the reaction also increases, but when all the active sites of the enzymes are occupied by the substrate molecules, then the rate of the reaction becomes constant; further increase in substrate concentration will not increase the rate of reaction.
  • iii) Temperature — The rate of an enzymatic reaction increases with increase in temperature. At optimum temperature the rate of the enzymatic reaction is maximum; the optimum temperature for human enzymes is 37°C. As the temperature increases above the optimum, the enzyme activity decreases; at very high temperature the enzyme becomes denatured and the rate of reaction decreases. Refrigeration lowers the temperature and the rate of enzyme activity in bacteria and fungi becomes low, so food does not spoil quickly in a refrigerator.
  • iv) pH — Enzymes work efficiently within a very narrow pH range. The pH at which the enzyme activity is maximum is called the optimum pH; it varies from enzyme to enzyme. For example, pepsin works best at pH 2.0 (in the stomach), whereas trypsin has an optimum pH of 8.0 (in the intestine). Activity of an enzyme decreases when the pH of a solution is away from the optimum pH of the enzyme.

Enzyme Inhibitors

The substance that can slow down or completely stop the enzyme activity is called an inhibitor. The use of penicillin (an antibiotic) is a very common example of enzyme inhibition: penicillin stops the growth of bacteria by inhibiting the enzymes which are involved in bacterial cell wall formation. Inhibitors may be:

  • i) Irreversible Inhibitors — These inhibitors combine with an enzyme by a covalent bond and inactivate the enzyme permanently.
  • ii) Reversible Inhibitors — These inhibitors combine with an enzyme by non-covalent bonds and inactivate the enzyme temporarily. Reversible inhibitors are of two types: a) Competitive inhibitors — the chemical structure of the competitive inhibitor is similar to the substrate, so it competes with the substrate and binds with the active site of the enzyme; the activity of the competitive inhibitor depends on its concentration, so by increasing the substrate concentration the effect of the competitive inhibitor can be reduced. b) Non-competitive inhibitors — these do not have a similarity with the substrate; they bind with the enzyme at a site other than the active site, called the allosteric site, and this binding changes the shape of the active site, so the enzyme becomes unable to bind with the substrate. The non-competitive inhibitors are not overcome by increasing the substrate concentration.

Key Points

  • Rate rises with enzyme and substrate concentration until the active sites saturate.
  • Optimum temperature for human enzymes is 37°C; high heat denatures enzymes. Pepsin works best at pH 2.0, trypsin at pH 8.0.
  • Competitive inhibitors fight for the active site; non-competitive inhibitors bind the allosteric site and change its shape.

lessons.notes_html:
ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate) is the energy currency of the cell. It is a nucleotide. It contains:

  • i) Adenine — A nitrogen base.
  • ii) Ribose — A five carbon sugar.
  • iii) Phosphate Group — Three phosphates.

Adenine and ribose combine to form adenosine. The phosphate groups are attached with ribose by high-energy bonds; these bonds are represented by a squiggle (∼), showing that a large quantity of energy is released by the hydrolysis of these bonds. The energy released during the hydrolysis of ATP is 7.3 Kcal/mole. ATP changes into ADP (Adenosine Diphosphate) and releases energy. ATP is formed by the energy released during the breakdown of glucose in the process of cellular respiration, and the energy of ATP is used in performing the metabolic activities of organisms.

How ATP Works

When a phosphate group is removed from ATP, energy is released and ADP is formed; when a phosphate group is added to ADP, energy is stored and ATP is formed again. In this way the cell keeps its energy in a ready-to-use form: ATP ⇄ ADP + energy. In cellular respiration, one molecule of glucose forms 36 molecules of ATP.

Key Points

  • ATP = adenine + ribose + three phosphates; its high-energy bonds are shown by a squiggle (∼).
  • Hydrolysis of ATP releases 7.3 Kcal/mole and forms ADP; adding a phosphate back stores energy again.

lessons.notes_html:
The word photosynthesis has been derived from two Greek words: "photo" means light and "synthesis" means putting together. Photosynthesis is a process by which green plants, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, use water and carbon dioxide to synthesize glucose (food).

6CO2 + 6H2O —(sunlight / chlorophyll)→ C6H12O6 + 6O2

Photosynthesis is an anabolic process. It is a unique process because it is the only process in the world which releases oxygen in the atmosphere. The importance of photosynthesis is that the life of all organisms depends upon it: all organisms depend upon autotrophs (photosynthetic organisms) for their food; heterotrophs take food from autotrophs. Photosynthesis has two phases: light reactions and dark reactions.

A. Light Reactions

Light reactions were studied by Hill in 1937. These reactions take place in the granum of chloroplasts in the presence of sunlight. The light reactions are:

  • i) Removal of Electrons — The chlorophyll molecules capture the energy of sunlight and remove electrons from chlorophyll molecules.
  • ii) Photolysis of Water — Water is broken down in the presence of sunlight; this process is called photolysis of water: H2O → 2H+ + 2e− + ½O2. During photolysis, oxygen is released.
  • iii) ATP Formation — The electrons removed from chlorophyll pass through an electron transport chain; during this process ATP is formed.
  • iv) NADPH2 Formation — The hydrogen ions (H+) produced from water join with electrons to form NADPH2. This NADPH2 is used in the dark reactions of photosynthesis.

B. Dark Reactions

Dark reactions were studied by Calvin, who got the Nobel Prize in 1961 for this work. The dark reactions take place in the stroma of the chloroplast; these reactions do not require sunlight directly. Dark reactions consist of three main stages:

  • i) Carbon Fixation — Carbon dioxide is incorporated into organic compounds; the CO2 from air (which has about 0.03–0.04% CO2) combines with a five-carbon compound called RuBP (Ribulose Bisphosphate). Three molecules of CO2 combine with three molecules of RuBP to form an unstable six-carbon compound, which immediately splits into six molecules of a three-carbon compound called PGA (Phosphoglyceric Acid).
  • ii) Reduction — In this step, PGA is converted into PGAL (Phosphoglyceraldehyde) by the use of ATP and NADPH2. PGAL is used in the formation of glucose.
  • iii) Regeneration — In this step, RuBP is regenerated from PGAL, so that the cycle can continue.

Key Points

  • Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O → glucose + 6O2; it is anabolic and releases oxygen.
  • Light reactions (Hill, 1937) occur in the granum: photolysis of water, ATP and NADPH2 formation.
  • Dark reactions (Calvin) occur in the stroma: fixation, reduction and regeneration of RuBP.

lessons.notes_html:
Respiration is a biological process in which food is broken down by oxidation to release energy. It is a redox reaction (oxidation + reduction). In a redox reaction, one reactant is oxidized (loses electrons) and the other is reduced (gains electrons).

Types of Respiration

  • A. Anaerobic Respiration — It occurs in the absence of oxygen and is also called fermentation. In anaerobic respiration, glucose is broken down incompletely, so only 2 ATP are formed. When anaerobic respiration occurs in yeast, ethanol (ethyl alcohol) and CO2 are produced; when anaerobic respiration occurs in bacteria and muscles, lactic acid is produced. The yogurt from milk is formed by the anaerobic respiration of bacteria.
  • B. Aerobic Respiration — It occurs in the presence of oxygen. In aerobic respiration glucose is broken down completely into CO2 and water, and 36 ATP are formed: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + 36 ATP (energy).

Mechanism of Aerobic Respiration

  • i) Glycolysis — The breakdown of glucose into pyruvic acid is called glycolysis. It takes place in the cytoplasm of the cell and does not require oxygen. In glycolysis, one molecule of glucose is converted into two molecules of pyruvic acid.
  • ii) Kreb's Cycle / Citric Acid Cycle — It takes place in the mitochondria. Pyruvic acid is converted into Acetyl-CoA by reacting with Co-enzyme A, and this Acetyl-CoA enters the Kreb's cycle, where it is completely oxidized into CO2 and water. ATP, NADH and FADH2 are formed during the Kreb's cycle.
  • iii) Electron Transport Chain — It takes place in the mitochondria. In this phase, the electrons present in NADH and FADH2 are passed through the electron transport chain; ATP is formed during this process, and oxygen combines with hydrogen to form water.

Key Points

  • Respiration is a redox reaction that releases energy from food.
  • Anaerobic respiration (fermentation) gives only 2 ATP; aerobic respiration gives 36 ATP.
  • Stages: glycolysis (cytoplasm), Kreb's cycle (mitochondria), electron transport chain (mitochondria).

lessons.notes_html:
There are about 8.7 million species of living organisms in this world. These organisms are different from each other in morphology, physiology, anatomy and behaviour. To understand the great variety of organisms present on earth, biologists have developed systems to organize and classify the biological diversity. In this chapter we will learn about biodiversity and its importance, the need for classification, history of classification, bases of classification, taxonomic hierarchy and binomial nomenclature.

Biodiversity

Biodiversity is a combination of two words: "bios" means life and "diversity" means variety. Thus biodiversity means the variety of life present on the earth, i.e. the variety of different species of organisms, their genes and the ecosystems in which they live. Biodiversity is not uniform on earth: the regions near the equator have the highest biodiversity, while the polar regions have very low biodiversity. Biodiversity of a region is affected by food, water, temperature, soil, altitude and climate etc.

Classification

The system of grouping organisms into different groups on the basis of similarities and differences is called classification. The branch of biology that deals with the classification of organisms is called taxonomy, and the scientist who studies taxonomy is called a taxonomist. The classification system helps in the identification of organisms, to study the relationships among them, and to understand their evolution.

Advantages of Classification

  • Classification helps us to identify the organisms and to study them in an organized way.
  • It gives us information about the similarities and differences among organisms.
  • It tells us about the common ancestry of organisms.
  • It helps to understand the relationships and evolution of organisms.

History of Classification

  • Aristotle (384–322 BC) — He was a Greek philosopher and is called the father of science. He classified organisms into two groups, i.e. plantae and animalia. He classified animals on the basis of habitat, i.e. aquatic, terrestrial and aerial.
  • Theophrastus (371–287 BC) — He is called the father of botany. He classified plants on the basis of morphology, i.e. trees, shrubs and herbs.
  • Abu-Usman Aljahiz (776–868 AD) — He was a Muslim zoologist. He wrote a famous book "Kitab Al-Hayawan" (Book of Animals), in which he described many animals and their behaviour.
  • Carolus Linnaeus (1707–1778 AD) — He was a Swedish botanist and is called the father of modern taxonomy. He classified organisms into two kingdoms, i.e. plantae and animalia. This system is called the two kingdom system of classification. But this system had some problems: for example, euglena has characteristics of both plants and animals, so it could not be placed properly in either kingdom.

Five Kingdom System

In 1969, Robert Whittaker proposed the five kingdom system of classification. The five kingdoms are: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. This classification is based on two main criteria: i) cellular organization (prokaryotic or eukaryotic, unicellular or multicellular) and ii) mode of nutrition (photosynthesis, absorption or ingestion). Later, in 1982, Margulis and Schwartz modified this system and renamed the kingdom Monera as Prokaryotae.

Key Points

  • Biodiversity = variety of life; classification groups organisms by similarities and differences (taxonomy).
  • Linnaeus gave the two kingdom system; Whittaker (1969) gave five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
  • Margulis and Schwartz (1982) renamed Monera as Prokaryotae.

lessons.notes_html:
All organisms are divided into two main groups on the basis of their cellular structure: prokaryotes and eukaryotes. The prokaryotes are further divided into two groups:

  • i) Archaebacteria — These are the ancient bacteria. They live in extreme environments like hot springs and salt lakes.
  • ii) Eubacteria — These are the true bacteria. They are found everywhere; some of them are useful, e.g. nitrogen fixing bacteria.

The eukaryotes include protista, fungi, plants and animals.

Three Domains

In 1977, Carl Woese proposed the three domain system of classification. According to this system, all organisms are divided into three domains:

  • i) Archaea — It includes archaebacteria (ancient bacteria).
  • ii) Bacteria — It includes eubacteria (true bacteria).
  • iii) Eukarya — It includes all eukaryotes, i.e. protista, fungi, plants and animals.

Archaea: The Extremophiles

Archaea are the organisms which live in extreme environments; they are also called extremophiles. They are of three types:

  • i) Methanogens — They produce methane gas.
  • ii) Halophiles — They live in highly salty environments.
  • iii) Thermoacidophiles — They live in hot and acidic environments.

Key Points

  • Carl Woese (1977) divided life into three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
  • Archaea are extremophiles: methanogens, halophiles and thermoacidophiles.

In classification, organisms are arranged in a hierarchy of groups called taxonomic ranks or categories. Each rank or category is called a taxon (plural: taxa). The main taxonomic ranks, from largest to smallest, are:

Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species

  • Genus — A group of closely related species.
  • Family — A group of related genera.
  • Order — A group of related families.
  • Class — A group of related orders.
  • Phylum — A group of related classes.
  • Kingdom — It is the highest taxonomic rank; a group of related phyla.

Binomial Nomenclature

Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving a scientific name to an organism, consisting of two parts: the first part is the genus name and the second part is the species name. This system was given by Carolus Linnaeus in 1753. For example, the scientific name of the mustard plant is Brassica campestris, in which Brassica is the genus and campestris is the species.

Rules of Binomial Nomenclature

  • The scientific name is in Latin or Greek language.
  • The genus name starts with a capital letter, while the species name starts with a small letter.
  • When handwritten, the scientific name is underlined; when printed, it is written in italics.

Some Scientific Names

Common NameScientific Name
PeaPisum sativum
MaizeZea mays
FrogRana tigrina
CatFelis catus
HumanHomo sapiens

Importance of Binomial Nomenclature

  • Common names of organisms are different in different languages and regions; for example, garlic is called lehson, thoom and ugga in different areas. The scientific name is the same all over the world.
  • Sometimes the same common name is used for different organisms; for example, rose is the common name of a flower, but it is also used for lichens. Scientific names avoid this confusion.
  • Scientific names show the relationship of organisms; for example, Felis catus (cat) and Felis leo (lion) belong to the same genus, so they are closely related.

Lichens are the organisms which are made up of a fungus and an alga living together.

Why Viruses Do Not Fit in the Classification System

Viruses are very small particles which can only be seen with an electron microscope. They are not included in the classification system of living organisms because they do not have cellular organization. Viruses remain inactive outside the host cell, but when they enter a living cell they become active and reproduce. Viruses are neither prokaryotes nor eukaryotes.

  • Living characteristics of viruses: they have nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) and they can reproduce inside the host cell.
  • Non-living characteristics of viruses: they have no protoplasm, they can be crystallized, and they do not respire.

Viruses have no cellular organization, and their mode of nutrition is not clear, so they do not fit in any kingdom of the classification system.

Key Points

  • Binomial nomenclature (Linnaeus, 1753): genus (capital) + species (small), in Latin/Greek, italic or underlined.
  • Scientific names are the same worldwide and show relationships between organisms.
  • Viruses have no cellular organization — they show both living and non-living characters, so they fit no kingdom.

lessons.notes_html:
Plants need nutrients for their growth and development. The nutrients which plants obtain from soil in the form of inorganic ions are called mineral nutrients. The study of how plants obtain and use mineral nutrients is called mineral nutrition. Water and minerals are absorbed by roots and transported to the leaves through xylem; this upward movement is called the ascent of sap, explained by the TACT mechanism (transpirational pull, adhesion, cohesion and tension). The food prepared in the leaves is transported to other parts of the plant through phloem; this transport of food is called translocation, explained by the pressure flow mechanism. In this chapter we study mineral nutrition, transport in plants, gaseous exchange, homeostasis and excretion in plants, osmotic adjustments, and reproduction in plants.

Mineral Nutrients

Plants absorb minerals from the soil in the form of ions. There are 16 elements which are vital for the normal growth of plants. On the basis of the quantity required, mineral nutrients are divided into two groups:

  • i) Macronutrients — These are required by plants in large amounts. There are 9 macronutrients: Carbon (C), Hydrogen (H), Oxygen (O), Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), Potassium (K), Sulphur (S), Calcium (Ca) and Magnesium (Mg).
  • ii) Micronutrients — These are required by plants in small amounts. There are 14 micronutrients, of which 7 are mostly required by plants: Boron (B), Chlorine (Cl), Copper (Cu), Iron (Fe), Manganese (Mn), Molybdenum (Mo) and Zinc (Zn). The other 7 micronutrients — Aluminium (Al), Cobalt (Co), Sodium (Na), Nickel (Ni), Selenium (Se), Silicon (Si) and Vanadium (V) — are required only in trace amounts by some plants.

Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are the main components of organic compounds. Carbon makes up about 18.5% of the human body, hydrogen about 9.5% and oxygen about 65%.

Role of Nitrogen and Magnesium

  • Nitrogen — Plants absorb nitrogen from the soil in the form of nitrates (NO3). Nitrogen is used in the synthesis of amino acids, which join to form proteins. Deficiency of nitrogen causes stunted growth of plants.
  • Magnesium — Magnesium is the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule. It also activates the enzymes which are involved in the synthesis of chlorophyll. Deficiency of magnesium causes chlorosis (yellowing of leaves).

Roles of Some Other Minerals

  • Phosphorus — It is needed for the formation of ATP, nucleic acids and cell membranes; it promotes root growth and flowering.
  • Potassium — It controls the opening and closing of stomata, activates enzymes, and helps in water balance and disease resistance.
  • Boron — It is needed for cell wall formation, flowering and seed setting.
  • Iron — It is needed for the formation of chlorophyll (though it is not a part of chlorophyll) and for electron transport in respiration and photosynthesis.

Key Points

  • 16 elements are vital for plants: 9 macronutrients (needed in large amounts) and micronutrients (needed in small amounts).
  • Nitrogen (absorbed as nitrates) builds amino acids and proteins; its deficiency stunts growth.
  • Magnesium is the central atom of chlorophyll; its deficiency causes chlorosis.

lessons.notes_html:
Transport in Plants

Plants need a transport system because they are multicellular organisms and the substances have to be moved over long distances. Water and minerals are transported through xylem, while food is transported through phloem.

Internal Structure of Root

The internal structure of a root, from centre to outside, is:

  • Xylem and Phloem — Present in the centre of the root; xylem transports water and minerals, phloem transports food.
  • Pericycle — A layer of cells around the vascular tissues.
  • Endodermis — A layer of cells inside the cortex.
  • Cortex — Made up of loosely packed cells; water passes through it.
  • Epidermis — The outermost single layer of cells.

Root Hairs and Absorption of Water

Root hairs are the extensions of the epidermal cells of the root. They have thin walls and increase the surface area of the root for absorption. The cell sap of root hairs has a higher concentration of salts than the soil water, so water enters the root hairs by osmosis.

Uptake of Water and Minerals

  • i) Passive Uptake — It occurs by diffusion and osmosis, without the use of energy. Water moves through the apoplast pathway (through cell walls and intercellular spaces) — this pathway is faster — or through the symplast pathway (through the cytoplasm of cells connected by plasmodesmata).
  • ii) Active Uptake — Minerals are absorbed against the concentration gradient, i.e. from lower concentration to higher concentration, by using energy (ATP). This is called active uptake or active transport.

Key Points

  • Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells; water enters them by osmosis.
  • Passive uptake uses no energy (apoplast and symplast pathways); active uptake uses ATP against the gradient.

lessons.notes_html:
Transpiration

The loss of water in the form of vapours from the aerial parts of the plant is called transpiration. Most of the transpiration (about 90%) occurs through the stomata of leaves; about 5% occurs through the cuticle and less than 3% through the lenticels. Transpiration through stomata occurs in two steps: first, water evaporates from the surface of mesophyll cells into the intercellular spaces; then the water vapours diffuse out of the leaf through the stomata. Stomata are generally open during the day and closed at night.

Factors Affecting Transpiration

  • Humidity — High humidity decreases the rate of transpiration, because the air is already saturated with water vapours.
  • Temperature — Increase in temperature increases the rate of transpiration; a rise of 10°C doubles the rate of transpiration. At very high temperature (above 40–45°C) the stomata close, so transpiration decreases.
  • Wind — Wind increases the rate of transpiration because it removes the water vapours from the surface of the leaf.

Ascent of Sap

The water absorbed by the roots is transported upwards to the leaves; this upward movement of water is called ascent of sap. The water present in the xylem vessels is called sap. The ascent of sap is explained by the TACT mechanism, given by Dixon and Jolly (Irish scientists) in 1894. TACT stands for:

  • T — Transpirational pull: the pulling force created by transpiration.
  • A — Adhesion: the attraction between water molecules and the walls of xylem vessels.
  • C — Cohesion: the attraction between water molecules themselves.
  • T — Tension: the pull exerted on the water column in the xylem.

Due to transpiration, a pull is created which pulls the water column upwards; the water is pulled, not pushed. The pathway of water is: soil → root hair → cortex → xylem → leaves → stomata. (Capillary action also helps water rise in narrow tubes like xylem vessels.)

Key Points

  • Transpiration is the loss of water vapours, about 90% through stomata; it rises with temperature and wind and falls with humidity.
  • Ascent of sap works by TACT — Transpirational pull, Adhesion, Cohesion, Tension (Dixon and Jolly, 1894).
  • Water is pulled up, not pushed: soil → root hair → cortex → xylem → leaves → stomata.

lessons.notes_html:
Translocation

The transport of food (sugars) from the leaves to other parts of the plant through phloem is called translocation. The phloem consists of sieve tube elements and companion cells. Food is transported in the form of sucrose.

Source and Sink

  • Source — The part of the plant where sugar concentration is high and food is prepared or stored, e.g. leaves. Food moves from the source.
  • Sink — The part of the plant where sugar concentration is low and food is used or stored, e.g. roots and fruits. Food moves towards the sink.

A storage organ acts as a sink when food is stored in it, and as a source when the stored food is used; for example, the root of sugar beet stores food (sink) and later provides it for growth (source).

Pressure Flow Mechanism

The pressure flow mechanism of translocation was given by Munch in 1930. Its steps are:

  • Glucose formed in the leaves is converted into sucrose.
  • Sucrose is pumped into the sieve tubes of phloem by using energy (ATP).
  • Water enters the sieve tubes from the xylem by osmosis, due to the high concentration of sucrose.
  • The hydrostatic pressure in the sieve tubes increases.
  • This pressure pushes the sucrose towards the sink.
  • At the sink, sucrose is unloaded and used or stored.
  • Water leaves the sieve tubes by osmosis, so the pressure decreases.

Key Points

  • Translocation moves sucrose through phloem from a source (leaf) to a sink (root, fruit).
  • Pressure flow mechanism (Munch, 1930): loading raises pressure, which pushes the food to the sink.

lessons.notes_html:
Gaseous Exchange in Plants

Plants have no special organ system for gaseous exchange; exchange of gases occurs by diffusion. Respiration occurs all the time (day and night), while photosynthesis occurs only during the day. In aquatic plants, gases are exchanged through wet surfaces. In land plants, gaseous exchange occurs through stomata (in leaves) and lenticels (loose cells in the cork or bark of stems). The air spaces among the spongy mesophyll cells also help in gaseous exchange. During the day, the CO2 produced in respiration is used in photosynthesis and the O2 produced in photosynthesis is used in respiration; at night, only respiration occurs, so O2 is taken in and CO2 is released. The loss of water in liquid form through special structures called hydathodes at night is called guttation.

Homeostasis in Plants

Plants maintain homeostasis by osmoregulation, thermoregulation and excretion. Homeostasis is important for plants because it helps in their survival, removes waste products, controls the opening and closing of stomata, and regulates the intake of CO2 and the release of O2.

Excretion in Plants

Plants have special adaptations to remove their waste products:

  • Excess water and gases are removed through stomata.
  • Calcium oxalate crystals are stored in cells, e.g. in tomato.
  • Resin is stored in pines.
  • Latex is stored in rubber plants.
  • Gums are produced by keeker (acacia) trees.
  • Old leaves fall off in autumn, removing wastes with them.
  • Wastes are also stored in the trunk as crystals, and in sepals, fruits and seed coats.
  • In aquatic plants, wastes diffuse out into the surrounding water.

Key Points

  • Plants exchange gases by diffusion through stomata and lenticels; guttation is liquid water loss through hydathodes.
  • Plant wastes are stored as crystals, resin, latex or gums, or shed with falling leaves.

lessons.notes_html:
Plants adjust to the water conditions of their habitat by special adaptations. On the basis of water availability, plants are divided into four groups:

  • i) Hydrophytes — Plants which live in water, e.g. water lily, hydrilla and lotus. Their xylem is poorly developed, leaves have a large surface area, stomata are many, and root hairs are absent.
  • ii) Mesophytes — Plants which live in areas with a moderate supply of water, e.g. rose, sheesham, mango and wheat. They control water loss by guard cells and cuticle.
  • iii) Xerophytes — Plants which live in dry areas (deserts), e.g. cactus and euphorbia. They are also called succulents. They have a thick cuticle, fewer stomata, water storing tissues, leaves modified into thorns, and deep and extensive root systems.
  • iv) Halophytes — Plants which live in salty water or soil, e.g. Rhizophora (mangrove) found in the Indus delta. The cell sap of halophytes is more concentrated (saltier) than the surroundings, so they can absorb water by osmosis. Some halophytes have salt glands to remove excess salt, e.g. sea milkwort, and their cell walls are thick and covered with mucilage.

Key Points

  • Hydrophytes live in water; mesophytes in moderate water; xerophytes in deserts; halophytes in salty places.
  • Halophytes keep their cell sap saltier than the surroundings and remove extra salt through salt glands.

lessons.notes_html:
Asexual Reproduction

Asexual reproduction is the type of reproduction in which a single parent produces offspring which are genetically identical to the parent. Its types are:

  • i) Binary Fission — The parent cell divides into two daughter cells. It occurs in prokaryotes, protozoans and algae: the DNA is copied and then the cell splits into two.
  • ii) Budding — A small outgrowth (bud) is formed on the parent body; the bud grows and detaches when mature to form a new individual. It occurs in yeast, and buds may stay attached to form colonies.
  • iii) Spore Formation — Spores are formed in special structures called sporangia, e.g. in Rhizopus (a fungus). Spores are tough and resistant; they can survive in unfavourable conditions and behave like seeds, germinating when conditions become favourable. It occurs in bacteria, fungi and non-flowering plants.
  • iv) Vegetative Propagation — New plants are produced from a fragment of the parent plant (root, stem or leaves). The new plants are clones and retain the desired characters of the parent.

Natural and Artificial Vegetative Propagation

Natural Vegetative PropagationArtificial Vegetative Propagation
Occurs without human intervention.Carried out by humans.
Occurs by roots, bulbs, corms, tubers and rhizomes.Occurs by cutting, layering and grafting.
It avoids the barriers of sexual reproduction.Desired characters are retained over generations.

Types of Vegetative Propagation

  • Bulb — A short underground stem with fleshy leaves, e.g. onion, daffodil, lily, tulip.
  • Corm — A solid underground stem, e.g. crocus, gladiolus, garlic.
  • Tubers — Stem tuber, e.g. potato; root tuber, e.g. sweet potato.
  • Suckers — Side shoots arising from the base of the stem, e.g. apple, cherry, banana, rose.
  • Rhizome — An underground stem, e.g. ginger, oak, grass, bamboo; in some plants the rhizome is above ground, e.g. ferns and irises.
  • Layering — A stem is bent and covered with soil while still attached to the parent; roots develop and a new plant is formed, e.g. climbing roses, raspberries, blackberries, grapes.
  • Runners / Stolons — Horizontal stems that grow along the ground and form new plants at nodes, e.g. grasses, strawberries.
  • Leaves — Some plants produce buds on the margins of leaves which develop into new plants, e.g. Begonia and Bryophyllum.

Artificial Methods

  • Grafting — A part of one plant (scion) is joined with the rooted part of another plant (stock). Oblique cuts are made and the two parts are tied together so that they fuse. It is used in roses, grapes, citrus and almond.
  • Stem Cutting — A piece of stem is cut and planted in soil, where it develops roots and grows into a new plant, e.g. sugarcane, roses, money plants.

Parthenogenesis and Cloning

  • Parthenogenesis — The development of an embryo from an unfertilized egg, without fertilization. It occurs in some fishes, amphibians, honey bees and aphids. In plants, the formation of fruit without fertilization is called parthenocarpy; it produces seedless fruits, e.g. banana and grapes.
  • Cloning — The production of a genetically identical copy of an organism from a single parental cell. In tissue culture, cells or tissues are grown in a germ-free nutrient medium to produce new plants.

Key Points

  • Asexual reproduction gives offspring identical to the single parent: fission, budding, spores, vegetative propagation.
  • Natural propagation uses bulbs, corms, tubers, suckers, rhizomes, runners and leaves; artificial methods are cutting, layering and grafting.
  • Parthenocarpy gives seedless fruits; tissue culture clones plants from cells in a nutrient medium.

lessons.notes_html:
Sexual Reproduction

In sexual reproduction, haploid gametes fuse to form a diploid zygote, which develops into a new organism. In the life cycle of plants there is an alternation of generations between the diploid sporophyte generation and the haploid gametophyte generation. The sporophyte (2n) is the dominant generation in flowering plants; it includes roots, stem, leaves and flowers.

Structure of a Flower

The flower is attached to the stem by a stalk called pedicel, and the top of the pedicel is called thalamus (a modified stem). Sepals are the green leaf-like structures which protect the flower in the bud stage. Petals are the coloured parts which attract insects for pollination. The stamen is the male reproductive part; it consists of a filament and a bilobed anther, in which microspores are produced by meiosis in the pollen sacs. The carpel is the female reproductive part; it consists of ovary, style and stigma. The ovary contains ovules, in which four megaspores are produced by meiosis, of which three degenerate.

Pollination and Gametophytes

The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma is called pollination; it is carried out by insects, wind or water. The male gametophyte is the pollen grain: on the stigma it germinates and forms a pollen tube; the generative nucleus divides to form two sperms, and the tube nucleus guides the tube. The female gametophyte (embryo sac) is present inside the ovule, which is covered by integuments and has an opening called micropyle; the central part is the nucellus. The embryo sac is 7-celled: it has 3 antipodal cells, a fusion (diploid) nucleus, 2 synergids and 1 egg cell.

Double Fertilization

In flowering plants, double fertilization takes place: one sperm fuses with the egg to form the zygote (2n), while the second sperm fuses with the diploid fusion nucleus to form the endosperm (3n), which provides food to the developing embryo. Double fertilization occurs only in angiosperms.

Seed and Fruit Formation

After fertilization, the ovule changes into the seed and the integuments form the seed coat (testa). The ovary wall develops into the fruit; the ripened ovary with seeds is called fruit.

Germination of Seed

The development of the embryo inside the seed into a new plant is called germination. It requires water, air (oxygen) and a suitable temperature. During germination the testa bursts; the radicle grows downwards to form the roots, and the plumule grows upwards to form the shoot.

Dispersal of Seeds and Fruits

  • By wind — Seeds are light and have hairs or wings, e.g. milkweed, maple, dandelion.
  • By water — Seeds and fruits can float, e.g. lotus, water lily, palm.
  • By animals — Seeds have hooks, awns or a sticky covering and attach to animal bodies, e.g. medicago and grasses; or they are eaten by animals and pass out undigested, e.g. cherry, blackberry, tomato.
  • By explosion — The fruit bursts open and throws the seeds out, e.g. broom, jewelweed, okra.

Key Points

  • The sporophyte (2n) is dominant; the flower's stamen makes microspores and the carpel's ovules make megaspores.
  • Double fertilization (only in angiosperms): sperm + egg → zygote (2n); sperm + fusion nucleus → endosperm (3n).
  • Ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit; germination needs water, air and suitable temperature.

lessons.notes_html:
All the species present on earth today have evolved from simple organisms that lived millions of years ago. All living organisms share a common ancestor. Evolution is the change in the characteristics of a species over several generations. Darwin described evolution as "descent with modification". The main driving force of evolution is natural selection. In this chapter we study the theories of evolution, Darwin's voyage and observations, natural selection, evidences of evolution, and speciation.

Theories of Evolution

  • i) Lamarck's Theory — Jean-Baptiste Lamarck proposed that organisms change during their life by the use and disuse of organs, and these acquired characteristics are passed on to the offspring. For example, the long neck of the giraffe developed because its ancestors stretched their necks to reach high leaves, and this character was inherited.
  • ii) Darwin's Theory — Charles Darwin proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection: organisms which are better adapted to the environment survive and reproduce, while the unfit are eliminated.
  • iii) Mutation Theory — Hugo de Vries proposed that new species arise suddenly by mutations — sudden changes in genes.

Darwin's Voyage

Charles Darwin travelled on a ship called HMS Beagle at the age of 22 years, from 1831 to 1837 (the book's dates). He visited South America and the Pacific islands. On the Galapagos Islands he observed giant tortoises: the tortoises of different islands were different from each other; they were about 4 feet long, weighed about 475 pounds, lived about 100 years and ate plants. He also observed finches: the beaks of finches on different islands were different, according to the food available on each island. After the voyage, Darwin spent 12 more years collecting facts and evidence, and then published his famous book "The Origin of Species".

Key Points

  • Evolution is "descent with modification"; natural selection is its main driving force.
  • Lamarck: use and disuse, inheritance of acquired characters. De Vries: sudden mutations make new species.
  • Darwin's Beagle voyage: Galapagos tortoises and finch beaks differed from island to island.

Evolution is a slow and gradual genetic change in a population over many generations; it does not occur in the lifetime of an individual.

Darwin and Wallace

Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently proposed the theory of natural selection. Their joint paper was presented in 1858–59. Darwin published his book "The Origin of Species by Natural Selection", in which he explained evolution by natural selection.

Observations of Darwin

  • i) Overproduction — Organisms produce far more offspring than can survive; for example, an oyster produces about 60 million eggs.
  • ii) Struggle for Existence — Resources like food and space are limited, so organisms struggle and compete with each other for survival, e.g. wolves compete for food.
  • iii) Variations — Individuals of a species show variations. Variations may be genetic or environmental. Useful variations are inherited by the offspring.
  • iv) Natural Selection (Survival of the Fittest) — Nature selects the organisms which are best adapted to the environment; they survive and reproduce, while the unfit perish.
  • v) Origin of New Species — Over many generations, the accumulated variations produce new species; for example, the 13 species of finches on the Galapagos Islands developed different beaks adapted to different foods.

Key Points

  • Darwin and Wallace jointly presented natural selection (1858–59).
  • Chain of evolution: overproduction → struggle for existence → variations → survival of the fittest → new species.

lessons.notes_html:
(i) Palaeontology — Fossil Evidence

Palaeontology is the study of fossils. Fossils provide direct evidence of evolution, because they show the organisms which lived in the past and how they changed over time. Archaeopteryx is a famous fossil which is a connecting link between reptiles and birds: it had reptilian characters (a toothed beak, a claw on the wing and a long tail) and avian characters (a wing with contour feathers forming an airfoil). This shows that birds evolved from reptiles.

(ii) Comparative Anatomy

  • Homologous Organs — Organs which have the same basic structure but perform different functions, e.g. the forelimbs of human, cat, whale and bat. They show common ancestry.
  • Analogous Organs — Organs which perform the same function but have different basic structure, e.g. the wings of insects, birds and bats.
  • Vestigial Organs — Organs which are reduced and functionless in an organism but were functional in its ancestors, e.g. the wings of kiwi and ostrich; in humans — the appendix, wisdom teeth, tail bone, ear muscles and nictitating membrane.

Selective Breeding

Humans have changed species in a short time by selective breeding (artificial selection): for example, the different breeds of dogs and pigeons, and improved varieties of crops like maize, wheat and tomato. This shows that species can change when selection acts on variations.

Key Points

  • Fossils are direct evidence: Archaeopteryx links reptiles and birds.
  • Homologous organs (same structure, different function) show common ancestry; analogous organs have the same function but different structure.
  • Vestigial organs like the human appendix are reduced remains of once-useful organs.

lessons.notes_html:
Sources of Variation

  • i) Mutation — A sudden change in the nucleotide sequence of DNA or in a gene produces new variations.
  • ii) Geographic Isolation — When a population is separated by a barrier like a mountain, river or ocean, the separated groups develop different variations.
  • iii) Hybridization — The crossing of two different species produces a hybrid with new characters, e.g. the zebroid, which is a cross between a horse and a zebra.
  • iv) Selective Breeding — Humans select organisms with desired characters and breed them, e.g. new varieties of wheat.

Species

A species is a group of organisms which have common characters and can interbreed with each other to produce fertile offspring.

Speciation

The formation of new species from existing species is called speciation. It occurs when a group of organisms of a species becomes separated from the rest of the species due to shortage of food, reproduction or geographic barriers. The separated group adapts to its new environment; over many generations, small differences accumulate, and eventually the group becomes so different that it forms a new species. The different beaks of the Galapagos finches are an example of speciation.

Key Points

  • Variation comes from mutation, geographic isolation, hybridization and selective breeding.
  • Speciation: a separated group adapts, differences accumulate over generations, and a new species forms.
